item.title: Making Your Rivals Depend on Your System Is How America Has Won for Three Centuries
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-ilt-让对手依赖你的体系-是美国赢了三百年的秘密/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-ilt-让对手依赖你的体系-是美国赢了三百年的秘密/
item.description: The Dutch, the British and the Americans took turns as hegemon not by blockading rivals but by getting them to stake their survival on someone else's maritime order — once they can't do without the sea lanes and the markets, cutting them off becomes the most effective weapon short of war.
item.content:encoded:
The Dutch, the British and the Americans took turns as hegemon not by blockading rivals but by getting them to stake their survival on someone else's maritime order — once they can't do without the sea lanes and the markets, cutting them off becomes the most effective weapon short of war.

Walter Mead breaks America's three-century winning streak into a five-step strategy and pushes it all the way to China, the Taiwan Strait and AI deterrence. What you get is a durable framework for judgment, not news-cycle opinion.

4:47 Unpredictability is a form of power
‘Unpredictability’ is not madness; it is a modern strategy of power. Mead says post-Cold War American diplomacy held itself up as a pillar of stability by ‘letting the whole world know where America's red lines are’, while Trump profits by doing the opposite: crossing lines, threatening allies, turning commitments into bargaining chips. He saw through a secret of the information age — the marginal cost of lying: the first lie is expensive, the thousandth is nearly free. When Clinton was engulfed by the Lewinsky scandal, he discovered that shame only lives in other people's minds; as long as you keep walking, the dogs bark and the caravan moves on. Trump took that insight to industrial scale. The cost is borne by the American diplomatic system: when the world's number one power turns itself into the unpredictable card, every alliance and rule built on predictability after World War II is coming apart faster.

10:00 The last step of global hegemony is cutting the cord
The Anglo-American maritime order did not win through some battle; it won through a five-step playbook. First, an open society on an island — the 17th-century Dutch tolerated heretics and Jews, and ideas and capital poured in. Then global trade: Dutch merchant ships sailed the world, and the wealth was so great that even the paintings are full of Turkish carpets and Brazilian parrots. Third, while continental powers fought over Silesia, you seized India and Canada across the globe. The fourth step is the riskiest: instead of copying Spain and sealing off your colonies, you invite the whole world in to do business, the British navy suppresses pirates, and every merchant ship benefits; Germany and Japan were likewise invited in after the war. Only the last step is the hole card: once the other side cannot do without your grain, your rubber and your shipping lanes, you cut it off — Germany discovered in World War I that Argentine grain and Malayan rubber had all been cut off, and its economy promptly collapsed.

16:38 Everything China does is to avoid having its cord cut
Look at China through the same framework and you find Beijing is well aware of its own vital point. Mead says: suppose the mainland blockades Taiwan, and the US counter-blockades from a hundred miles off Taiwan's coast: oil cannot get in, manufactured goods cannot get out, soybean contracts with Brazil and Argentina are voided, and China's economy is strangled alive. He has discussed these things with officials and scholars at Chinese universities, and this worry is always present. So China's energy policy has to be read side by side: on one hand it builds oil reserves so large they surprise outsiders; on the other it races into solar and hydropower while digging as much coal as it can. Not schizophrenia — the same single project: pulling out, one by one, the soft spots of ‘dependence on the outside world’. He also warns the US not to retreat into isolationism — agriculture and AI both need overseas markets to feed themselves.

25:50 Every round of technological bounty needs a new institution to match
Mead starts from the ownership society: at America's founding there were independent farmers with land everywhere, and while a bridge is nice it means my taxes go up — that trade-off is itself a political education. The railroad era came with the Homestead Act, the government giving land to railroad companies and farmers, and a national market grew out of it; in the 20th century what replaced the family farm was the single-family suburban house, paired with tax-exempt municipal bonds and highways, becoming the new wealth-distribution machine. Now that machine has hit housing prices: young people cannot afford to live near where they work. His remedy is remote work and autonomous driving. When the commuting radius expands from 40 miles to 75 miles, usable land for housing rises with the square of the radius, and the physical space opened by technology is enough to carry two more generations. But the precondition is filling in the institutional ‘infrastructure’ — he coined the word info-structure for the institutions and regulatory rules that let AI actually land in hospitals and courts.

40:22 Silicon Valley is going over to the Tech Hamiltonian camp
American foreign policy debate has for centuries been four vocabularies: Hamiltonians want a strong state clearing the way for capital, Wilsonians want to spread liberal democracy, Jeffersonians fear a bigger government, Jacksonians stay isolationist in peacetime and hit to kill when struck. The post-Cold War establishment was a marriage of Hamilton and Wilson, but Trump brought Jefferson and Jackson into the room. Mead says the new species really worth watching is the Tech Hamiltonian. In the 1990s tech companies loved to say ‘we are a global company, Google has no borders, Washington has no say’; AI competition has turned tech into a contest of national destiny. Economic positions changed too: the old multinational car companies wanted borderless labor and markets, while Silicon Valley wants supply-chain and IP security, and even wants its employees patriotic — selling code to China is shameful, and your colleagues will report you. The core of business has shifted from the old multinationals to tech nationalists, and this is the underwater current of America's political realignment.

50:00 The power with the most equipment fears technological turnover most
Mead has been to Ukraine twice. The first time he visited a drone factory and saw them converting children's toy trucks into ground drones that carry mines to blow up tanks; months later he went again, and the progress was unimaginably fast. The battlefield is now a gray kill zone, usually only two or three soldiers move together, and one of the hardest problems is ‘how do you get the wounded out’ — you need a ground drone with a metal shield to drag a person, plus a squad of drones hunting the enemy drones coming to attack it. He heard of one wounded soldier who took 63 days to be evacuated from the front. The situation flips every six months. The bitter irony for the US: the power with the most tanks and aircraft carriers is precisely the one that fears this kind of parameter revolution most — existing equipment turns from an advantage into a relocation cost. Russia's Black Sea Fleet has no great battle to fight, yet it is bottled up at home by Ukrainian small boats and drones.

54:16 The new variable most worth watching in the Taiwan Strait is Japan
On whether the mainland will attack Taiwan, Mead's judgment is that Beijing needs a very high probability of success before it will cross the threshold — failure would be catastrophic for the initiator. But between ‘attack’ and ‘do nothing’ there is a long gray ladder: for instance requiring all merchant ships bound for Taiwan to first call at mainland ports for customs clearance, or imposing a soft blockade — moves that change facts on the ground enough without triggering an armed US response. The real new variable on the Taiwan board is not America's attitude but Japan. The Japanese have already said publicly that if China takes Taiwan, Japanese independence is finished too; they are raising defense budgets, rewriting security doctrine, reshaping the national psyche. Historically Japan turns very fast when faced with a real threat. How steep Japan's learning curve is, and whether Beijing must factor Japan into its calculations, is the key to the Taiwan question in the coming years.

1:10:00 AI actually makes deterrence more credible
Moving Cold War deterrence logic into the algorithmic age, Mead points to a counterintuitive corollary: deterrence succeeds or fails on making the opponent one hundred percent believe that ‘if I do X, you will necessarily do Y, and you can do it and are willing to’. As long as there is a human veto point in the decision chain — ‘I might go soft when the time comes’ — that commitment has a crack in it. Automating part of foreign-policy decision-making and handing it to AI turns retaliation into an executable mechanism that will not hesitate — deterrence becomes more credible. But this is the doomsday machine problem from science fiction: decisions of civilizational scale no longer require a human to bear the consequences. His own assessment of the question is ‘very interesting and a little confusing’, and he does not think the answer has appeared yet.

item.title: ECT Is Not What You Think: A Century of Drift from Back Room to Routine Treatment
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-tpwky-ect-不是你想的那样-从密室到常规治疗的百年漂移/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-tpwky-ect-不是你想的那样-从密室到常规治疗的百年漂移/
item.description: Modern ECT is a procedure performed under anesthesia and muscle relaxants, with strong efficacy, but the evidence on memory-loss side effects remains incomplete, and social misunderstanding has left it over-stigmatized.
item.content:encoded:
Modern ECT is a procedure performed under anesthesia and muscle relaxants, with strong efficacy, but the evidence on memory-loss side effects remains incomplete, and social misunderstanding has left it over-stigmatized.

If your image of ECT is still stuck on One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, this episode will completely reset it. Hear the actual procedure, the indications, the side effects, and one expert's clinical account.

8:07 What actually happens if you or I get ECT
If you or I were to receive ECT, here is how it goes: first a risk assessment and informed consent, then a physical exam, then an overnight fast. The next morning, in a hospital or outpatient setting, an IV line is placed and two blood pressure cuffs are put on (arm and right leg), with EKG, EEG and EMG hooked up. After the anesthesiologist puts you to sleep, the leg cuff is inflated to restrict blood flow to the right foot, then a muscle relaxant (such as succinylcholine) is given. Once the muscles are fully relaxed, a bite block is placed, and then a brief pulse of current is delivered through the electrodes (lasting seconds, even half a second). The goal is not to make your whole body convulse, but to induce a generalized seizure, typically lasting 25-70 seconds. Because the muscles are relaxed, you see almost no external movement — the whole thing is obvious on the EEG.

14:15 Electrode placement, and why the right side comes first
There are several electrode placements: bitemporal (like in the movies), bifrontal, and most commonly 'right unilateral' — one electrode on the right temple, the other on the right side of the top of the head. Right unilateral is used for most people because it produces fewer cognitive side effects. Why consider the right side first? Because for about 98% of right-handed people and 70%-90% of left-handed people, language function sits in the left temporal lobe. Avoiding electrical stimulation on the left side theoretically reduces language-related memory problems. But right unilateral is slightly less effective than bilateral. During treatment, doctors switch based on side effects and efficacy: if bilateral side effects are heavy, switch to right unilateral; if right unilateral is not working well, switch to bilateral.

16:20 Seizure threshold and the effective dose
The seizure threshold is the minimum amount of current that can induce a seizure. There is no precise measuring device, so you start by estimating from age, then probe upward from a low dose until a seizure appears. But treatment does not stop at merely reaching threshold — the effective dose is usually 2.5 to 5 times the threshold. With bilateral, 2.5 times is enough, while right unilateral needs 5 times, because unilateral stimulation has a harder time achieving the same effect. The dose varies from person to person and has to be adjusted as you go. If in one session a patient's seizure does not occur or does not last long enough (less than 25 seconds), the doctor may increase the dose and try again. Treatment is generally three times a week, with a full course of 6 to 18 sessions, sometimes longer.

20:22 We still do not know exactly how ECT works
Why does shocking the brain treat depression and catatonia? Frankly: we still do not fully understand. There are several main hypotheses. One is neurotransmitter change: after ECT, serotonin, dopamine and GABA (an inhibitory transmitter) all change markedly. The rise in GABA is itself anticonvulsant, which could explain why the seizure threshold rises and seizures get shorter over a course of treatment. Two, large hormonal fluctuations are seen in the hypothalamus and pituitary — ACTH, prolactin, TSH and others. Three, ECT promotes neurogenesis, with BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) as a key molecule. But how these changes directly relieve symptoms still has no one-to-one mechanism. The mechanism may also differ by illness (depression, schizophrenia, catatonia), so for now the only option is to keep researching.

24:24 Depression data: far better than first-line antidepressants
For treating severe depression, ECT's key data are quite strong: most studies report remission rates (symptoms fully gone) of 50%-60% and response rates (symptoms clearly improved) of 60%-90%. By comparison, the best remission rate for SSRI antidepressants is only about 40%. ECT has another uncommon benefit — it can cut the 30-day readmission rate in half. This is not to say it should be first choice, nor that it has no risks (relapse or symptom rebound within 6-12 months is still not rare); but in patients with treatment-resistant depression combined with severe suicide risk, these efficacy advantages are hard to ignore.

26:27 Among side effects, memory problems draw the most concern
ECT's thorniest side effects center on cognition and memory. Right after the procedure there is brief confusion lasting from a few dozen seconds to half an hour, and for weeks there may be declines in attention and executive function. Interestingly, most cognitive function actually improves in the long term — possibly because the depression improves. The real trouble is memory. Anterograde amnesia (difficulty forming new memories) mostly recovers within a few weeks after the course ends, which is why many people are restricted from driving or making major decisions during treatment. Retrograde amnesia (losing past memories) is what worries patients more: it usually affects recall of the most recent months or even years before treatment, and in most cases recovers, but in some it is permanent. Bilateral treatment is more prone to this problem than right unilateral.

34:55 Catatonia: a lethal syndrome that gets misread
Catatonia is often simply lumped in as a subtype of schizophrenia, but it is actually a psychomotor syndrome that any psychiatric or neurological illness can trigger. Patients appear awake, eyes open, yet are almost completely motionless and mute; they may show posturing, waxy flexibility (an arm placed in a position does not fall). Because they cannot eat or drink and do not move for long periods, they are prone to malnutrition, pressure sores, muscle contractures, and even death. Untreated catatonia has a mortality rate as high as 20%! The most common treatment is benzodiazepines, but ECT is extremely effective in catatonia from many causes. The girl with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis mentioned earlier (the 'Brain on Fire' case) developed catatonia, and when both immunotherapy and lorazepam failed, she ultimately recovered with ECT.

48:36 The biggest bottleneck is not efficacy but access
Dr. Lopez believes the biggest obstacle ECT currently faces is finding a place to get treated. His hospital performs more than 6,000 treatments a year across two campuses, averaging about 10-12 per patient. But it is not widely available across the US, and adults and children traveling across state lines for care are not few — especially in infants, children and adolescents with catatonia from autoimmune encephalitis, where finding an experienced treatment team is extremely hard. So improving access is his greatest hope. At the same time, doctors on other internal medicine, pediatric and critical care teams often do not recognize catatonia and do not dare, or do not think, to call an ECT consult; so 'preaching' to non-psychiatric colleagues is part of his daily work.

item.title: The Supreme Court Gave Students Constitutional Rights, Then Handed Searches and Paddlings Back to the Schools
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-stuffmissed-美国最高法院先给了学生宪法权利-后来又把搜包和体罚还给校园/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-stuffmissed-美国最高法院先给了学生宪法权利-后来又把搜包和体罚还给校园/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: From refusing to salute the flag to having a purse searched, six cases gradually drew the constitutional rights of American public school students; the Supreme Court laid down that "schools are not totalitarian enclaves" while also upholding corporal punishment and reasonable-suspicion searches, narrowing the boundary of those rights.
item.content:encoded:
From refusing to salute the flag to having a purse searched, six cases gradually drew the constitutional rights of American public school students; the Supreme Court laid down that "schools are not totalitarian enclaves" while also upholding corporal punishment and reasonable-suspicion searches, narrowing the boundary of those rights.

Each case gets five or six minutes laying out the background and the holding, suited to listeners who want to grasp in one sitting the boundaries of speech, corporal punishment and searches in American public schools.

5:10 The flag-salute case: student rights enter the school for the first time
Can students really invoke the First Amendment during the school day? This case actually begins with religion: Jehovah's Witnesses families held that saluting the flag violated the commandments against having other gods and against graven images, and refused to pledge or salute the flag. In 1940 the Supreme Court had ruled against them, and World War II pushed more school districts to require students to salute and recite the pledge daily. West Virginia expelled students who refused the pledge, labeled them delinquents, and their parents could be fined or even jailed. In 1943 the Supreme Court overturned the earlier ruling 6-3, and Justice Jackson wrote the opinion on Flag Day: orthodoxy in politics, nationalism, religion or other matters of opinion is not to be defined by any official; students need not utter words they do not believe, nor make empty gestures. This was the first time the Court established that students hold some First Amendment rights inside school.

11:21 An official prayer text is ruled unconstitutional
In the Cold War the United States cast itself as a God-fearing nation, added "Under God" to the Pledge of Allegiance in 1954, and more public schools began reading scripture or praying before class. In 1951 the New York State Board of Regents asked religious leaders to co-write a short, non-denominational prayer, with each district deciding whether to adopt it. Districts that used the prayer let students opt out, but the parents of 10 students still sued. In 1962 Engel v. Vitale held it unconstitutional 6-1; the key was not whether it was compulsory but that the prayer was written by the government, which itself amounted to establishing religion. Justice Black quoted Madison: the first experiment on our liberties should call forth the alarm; the same authority that could establish Christianity to the exclusion of other religions could easily establish one Christian sect. The ruling provoked fierce backlash, and the plaintiff families were mocked and harassed.

18:31 An armband is constitutional expression
In December 1965, middle and high school students in Des Moines planned to wear black armbands to class to protest American involvement in the Vietnam War. School officials announced in advance that refusal to remove them would mean suspension, and some students — including four siblings — wore the armbands anyway and were suspended. In 1969 the Supreme Court ruled for the students 7-2. The issue was that this was not ordinary dress or grooming but quiet, passive expression close to pure speech, and it did not disrupt class. Absent evidence of actual disruption or a provable likelihood of substantial interference with teaching, school officials may not suppress student opinion. The ruling said: public schools may not become totalitarian enclaves, and students and teachers do not shed their constitutional rights at the schoolhouse gate. This "substantial disruption" standard later became the baseline for free speech on campus. Justice Black dissented that students would from then on resist almost every school rule, and the host said on the show that this slippery-slope argument sounds rather absurd.

24:40 A school-funded newspaper can be censored
In 1983 two pieces in the Hazelwood East High School student newspaper The Spectrum troubled principal Reynolds: a story on teen pregnancy that used pseudonyms but might still make the interviewees identifiable, and a divorce story that named and criticized a student's parent. Reynolds decided to cut both full pages rather than just remove the articles, on the grounds that he had no time to revise and the paper had to come out before the semester ended. In 1988 the Supreme Court ruled for the school 5-3. The key distinction was between "tolerating student speech" and "promoting student speech": this paper was funded and published by the school, readers would take its contents as endorsed by the school, and the two pieces were indeed ethically immature journalism. The Court held that school officials may exercise control over what they promote. The rights established in Tinker thus acquired their first clear boundary.

29:46 Corporal punishment is not an Eighth Amendment matter
Host Tracy suddenly recalled that many of her teachers kept wooden paddles on their desks, and on looking it up found that corporal punishment has still not died out in the United States. In the 1977 case Ingram v. Wright, the school's rule specified a paddle under two feet long, three or four inches wide and half an inch thick, in principle one to five swats; but Ingram was struck more than 20 times in a single incident and needed medical attention. The Supreme Court did not dwell on whether that instance was excessive, but held that school corporal punishment does not violate the Constitution. The reasoning: the Eighth Amendment protects the convicted, and prisoners are separated from schoolchildren by "the harsh facts of criminal conviction and incarceration"; schools are open places, with teachers and classmates as witnesses, and the child goes home at the end of the day. According to NEA figures, corporal punishment remains legal in public schools in 17 states and is actually practiced in 14, with boys, Black students and students with disabilities struck at significantly higher rates.

33:52 A search of a bag needs only reasonable suspicion
In 1980 a 14-year-old student known as TLO in New Jersey was reported by a teacher for smoking in the restroom. Vice principal Choplik searched her purse, saw cigarettes and rolling papers, kept digging, and found what appeared to be marijuana and evidence of drug dealing; TLO was ultimately convicted and given a year's probation. In 1985 the Supreme Court upheld the search 6-3. The ruling acknowledged that the Fourth Amendment binds school officials and that students have a privacy expectation, but that it must be balanced against the school's need to maintain a learning environment. So school searches need not meet the probable cause required of police; the lower threshold of reasonable suspicion suffices. The teacher's report that TLO was smoking gave the vice principal reason to suspect she had cigarettes, and a purse is exactly the obvious place; seeing rolling papers naturally extended the suspicion to marijuana, which was equally reasonable.

item.title: To Make Criticism Land, Lead With High Standards and Trust
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-thinkfast-批评想被听进去-先给高期待与信任/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-thinkfast-批评想被听进去-先给高期待与信任/
item.description: Getting criticism believed isn't about opening with a few compliments — it's about letting the other person see that the standard is high and that you believe they can reach it. item.content:encoded:
Getting criticism believed isn't about opening with a few compliments — it's about letting the other person see that the standard is high and that you believe they can reach it. In one experiment, a single line — "the standard is high but you can get there" — pushed Black students' rate of actually revising their essays to the highest of any condition.

The originator of stereotype threat research breaks down the mechanism himself and grounds the intervention in a replicable experimental script. Twenty minutes of high information density, with none of the vague communication chicken soup.

1:04 Identity bias makes people underperform on the spot
When a situation carries a negative label about one of your identities, and that situation matters to you, you worry about being judged by that label. That worry comes from the situation itself: it depresses performance in tests, sports or intellectual tasks on the spot, and it makes people avoid such situations over the long run, which in turn shapes who they befriend, where they live, and where they send their kids to school. The anxiety doesn't come from ability — it comes from the expectation of being defined by the label.

3:10 Social media lets labels chase you from every side
Social media's power lies in how fast it spreads thumbnail sketches of what a group is like. People have no patience to see the full picture and the exceptions, so it naturally multiplies the number of situations in which you might be seen through your identity. Occasionally it also spreads images that reduce threat, but the overall tone skews negative. The result is that in a diverse society, everyone is more alert to their own identity and to what others might be thinking.

6:16 A 15-minute self-affirmation exercise lifts grades
In racially integrated classrooms, Black students live with the constant possibility that their ability is being underestimated. Teachers simply asked seventh graders to spend 15 minutes writing a short essay about the people and things they valued most. White students were barely affected, but Black students used the occasion to let the teacher know "I'm not just that label," and their grades began to rise — feeding a positive loop: better grades → less vigilance about the label → still better grades. The intervention costs almost nothing, yet it changes a long-term trajectory.

9:20 Vigilance in diverse settings: remember or forget
The author calls this state churn. In settings where people of different backgrounds are together and the outcome matters, people are pulled back and forth between two choices: remember that "others might read me through my group's stereotype" to protect themselves, or simply forget it, relax, and trust the person in front of them. This isn't fragility — it's real pressure the situation creates. When the setting matters, it continuously drains attention that should be going to the task.

12:24 High standards plus trust make feedback work
In the experiment, students wrote an essay about their favorite teacher and received critical feedback. Under the first two approaches — giving it straight, or first putting on a "positive hat" — white students trusted the feedback, while Black students were highly distrustful of both. The third approach merely added one sentence: "We have high standards, because these essays are going to be published; I read your essay and I believe you can reach them." Under that condition, Black students took their essays home to revise at three times the rate of the other conditions.

14:26 You can't assume others already trust you
After years as a dean and provost, Claude considers the most useful skill to be realizing that everyone you work with needs that signal of respect. Society's common mistake is to assume trust is already there, when in reality people worry about how you see the group they belong to. Truly effective leaders are good at giving that signal first: even if an employee disagrees with a decision, as long as they feel the other person respects who they are and their potential, the team atmosphere is completely different.

17:35 Let people see you're human before you talk trust
Claude breaks good communication into three things: first, let the other person know you understand what this situation means to them — when power is unequal, the person with more power has to send the safety signal first; second, near-paranoid clarity, because beating around the bush destroys valuable information; third, warmth and goodwill, because people need to confirm that the person across from them is a good person before they hand over trust. Matt sums it up as connect, be clear, care.

item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-econtalk-拉丁文练不出外科医生-考试难-不如考得有用/

item.description: Latin doesn't make surgeons: skills barely transfer. If you assume "harder means better brain training," a nation's brightest get wasted on the most useless knowledge — that is the lesson of the Qing examination system.
item.content:encoded:
Latin doesn't make surgeons: skills barely transfer. If you assume "harder means better brain training," a nation's brightest get wasted on the most useless knowledge — that is the lesson of the Qing examination system.

It puts imperial civil-service exams, military selection and modern transfer experiments on a single chain of evidence, unusually connecting history with talent assessment — and the two sides genuinely clash.

10:03 Wrong exam content dooms the country, however smart the candidates
Hong Xiuquan failed the Qing examinations at least four times. After the last failure, on the road home, he had a vision, believed himself the brother of Christ, and eventually launched the Taiping Rebellion — which Daisy says may be the bloodiest civil war in human history, with deaths around thirty million. Hong was not alone among failures: examination seats were far fewer than the number of candidates, many sat the exams into their forties and fifties without passing, and the only way home was to teach. Daisy adds that the deeper cost fell on those who passed: they were masters of the eight-legged essay yet knew nothing of the science and mathematics then transforming the world. When the brightest young men can only practise a dead format, the country bleeds from both directions at once.

22:51 British civil-service reform was elites reproducing themselves
The Northcote-Trevelyan report is often seen by the British as the founding document of the modern civil service, but Daisy backs the revisionist judgment: under the name of a unified exam, it pushed Oxford and Cambridge classics graduates into key posts. Benjamin Jowett, master of Balliol, worked behind the scenes to place his classics students throughout the empire. Michael Coolican's "No Tradesmen and No Women" points out that the 1854 report reduced the most naked buying and selling of offices, but also snuffed out the professional exams that departments had been growing. Exams are not incapable of selecting people; what they test decides whether they select the worthy or select people like oneself.

35:58 A bureaucracy without price signals corrects itself through corpses
Daisy attributes bureaucratic failure to the absence of feedback: no price mechanism, no profit and loss, so a department cannot tell whether its program saves or kills. The military sounds like a counterexample, but military bureaucracies err just as constantly in peacetime; almost every time Britain went to war after a long peace, a crisis brewed in the first year, as with the shell crisis at the start of World War I. What actually forces correction then is not internal inspection but mass death on the battlefield. She calls it a correction mechanism crueler than prices. To make a bureaucracy reliable, you must first create a signal that lets consequences be seen; otherwise no severity of selection can save the quality of everyday decisions.

43:06 The Royal Navy won by testing navigation, not Latin
Daisy notes that the real pillar of Victorian Britain was not the army but the Royal Navy. As early as 1677, after the navy kept losing to the Dutch, Samuel Pepys set an oral exam for captains: three senior officers questioned them face to face on how to command a ship. Over the following century and more, navigation, charting and trigonometry entered the written exams, and chart-makers like Nelson, Cook, Flinders and Bligh all passed through that gate. Daisy uses this to draw out two exam traditions: what Pepys tested was the skill needed right away; what Macaulay and Northcote-Trevelyan later wanted to test was the classical languages. One served safety at sea, the other served a barrier of status, and the effects naturally differed.

47:31 Content doesn't matter? Macaulay's screening argument misses a key link
Here comes the highlight of the whole session: Daisy reads aloud Macaulay's 1833 speech in Parliament. The gist is that whatever a age happens to teach, the best at it must be the cleverest, most industrious and most honor-seeking of the young; so Cambridge could teach Ptolemy instead of Newton and its top students would still be excellent; teach Cherokee in place of Greek and the best Cherokee scholar would still be a man of parts; even astrology and alchemy would do. Another MP immediately praised it as the speech of most practical wisdom in parliamentary history, but Daisy says flatly: this is more like being carried away by one's own eloquence, and it misses entirely that "what you learn really does matter."

51:21 Dead twigs and corn: wrong content makes discipline just watering
Daisy closes out Macaulay with the 1917 rebuttal of the American medical educator Abraham Flexner. Flexner said the devotees of mental training are like Egyptian priests: they stick a row of dead twigs in the soil and then water them on schedule for the sake of discipline. Plant corn and the discipline is no less, with a crop thrown in. Against the American medical schools of the day, where many aspiring doctors were forced to read Greek and Latin before they were allowed near a medical book, Flexner's answer was: medicine is already hard enough, and using it to sharpen the mind is far more efficient than using ancient languages. Daisy agrees: spend the best years of the most gifted on what has been disproved or is useless, and the only winner is the rival whose young people learn real knowledge.

59:21 Rectangles don't train triangles: transfer needs identical elements
Thorndike designed a cleaner controlled experiment: have people repeatedly estimate the area of rectangles, let them improve markedly, then have them estimate the area of triangles — and almost nothing transfers. Even with two shapes that close, the result holds, so the claim that classical languages sharpen the mind is even less credible. Thorndike's explanation was identical elements: transfer appears only when old and new tasks share the same components; far transfer essentially breaks down. From this Daisy derives a principle of exam design: to select people who can navigate, test navigation and trigonometry; to select people who can practise medicine, test medicine. An exam that actually works wires its difficulty directly to the real task.

item.title: Global liquidity peaks: the companies that spent most aggressively on AI in the first half are the first to be discounted
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-cn38ff4a-全球流动性见顶-上半年越激进砸-ai-的公司-越先被折价/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-cn38ff4a-全球流动性见顶-上半年越激进砸-ai-的公司-越先被折价/
item.description: A rising capital market needs new money to keep taking the other side. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that invested most aggressively in AI in the first half are shifting from being rewarded to being discounted.
item.content:encoded:
A rising capital market needs new money to keep taking the other side. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that invested most aggressively in AI in the first half are shifting from being rewarded to being discounted.

It puts US AI capex, Hong Kong IPO subscriptions and household balance sheets on the same funding chain — a macro framework that does not treat AI as a panacea.

0:33 A low IPO break rate is not a good signal
Do not read the low first-day break rate of Hong Kong IPOs as a strengthening market. In the first half of this year the break rate was only in the teens, far below the roughly fifty-fifty level that a market-based mechanism would produce — meaning the money subscribing to new listings is mainly short-term speculative arbitrage, not long-term investors. Recently the supply of new listings has shrunk and IPO-related funds have blown up, yet the two most recent listings still broke issue price, showing that temporary supply-side control has not solved the underlying problem: Hong Kong faces the same liquidity peak.

12:07 The more aggressive the AI spending, the sooner the punishment
Market attitude reversed within a single quarter. Before Q1, the capital market rewarded aggression: the louder the AI CapEx talk, the higher the valuation. By the time half-year reports were disclosed in late July, any large internet company that had made aggressive capital expenditures in the first half — especially those that burned through free cash flow — was discounted, and even Google was not exempt. Q2 was precisely the quarter of maximum FOMO across the whole supply chain, with everyone rushing to spend before prices rose, and inventory still able to hold up gross margins; by Q3, when inventory is exhausted and price increases feed back in, the negative factors will show up together.

15:54 Nvidia is closer to Cisco in 2000
Nvidia's earnings look good, but its cash flow is changing shape. Before the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, Cisco rolled out rent-to-own arrangements to help customers finance purchases, pulling future revenue forward into current sales revenue; Nvidia is now pushing rent-to-own as well. In its financials, free cash flow halved quarter over quarter, and receivables on the books are far above historical levels — which is suspected to be partly related to the credit enhancement and collection structure that rent-to-own brings. Nvidia may therefore have reached a stage where it needs more aggressive financial engineering to sustain capital-market expectations, a situation with similarities to Cisco back then.

33:21 Primary-market money is bullets from three years ago
The answer lies in when the funds were raised. The money being deployed into AI and robotics in the second half of 2025 and the first half of 2026 mainly comes from funds raised at the market peak in 2020-2022; from 2023 to 2025 they barely invested, until they saw state capital placing bets during a period when no one dared to invest and earning the most — the stories of ChangXin and ChangCun, two large models and two large chips stimulated market-based capital, and the mindset became: copy the state capital's homework. So this is not a rational long-term incremental wave; it looks more like a delayed emotional release.

47:31 The new property policy detaches households from the financing chain
The key to recent real estate policy is not bailing out developers but pulling households out of the old financing loop. Buying a pre-sale home used to mean the household played the role of financing counterparty in the investment-driven chain: pay first, receive the home later; by pushing the chain toward a market-based model, the policy means buyers get completed homes and bear only the consumer role, with risk reset back onto developers and financing institutions. The policy was introduced when home prices were near the bottom in order to first stabilise the denominator on the asset side, avoiding panic from dismantling the chain during a decline. Japan after the 1990s and the consolidation of China's coal and mining industries followed similar paths.

1:01:34 A slow bull is not a slogan, it is a chip structure
A slow bull does not come from shouting; it comes from layering market chips by duration: at the bottom, low-valuation high-dividend blue chips taken up by insurers as long money that rarely trades; above that, mutual funds and index funds performing a quasi-stabilisation function; above that, Central Huijin and China Securities Finance adjusting the index; and only at the top, retail investors, private funds and active managers. The new insurance rules require liabilities and assets to match on maturity, yield and liquidity — institutionally ensuring long money invests long, medium money invests medium and short money invests short: you are not allowed to take ordinary people's short money and put it into ten-year illiquid assets.

1:22:49 Crises get bigger with each rescue, and bubbles at least one and a half times
After the dollar left gold in 1971, global central banks became increasingly accustomed to intervening directly in crises by printing money, each time faster than the last. The quantitative easing after 2008 should have been cleared out during the rate-hiking cycle, but political intervention cut it short, and then came the pandemic in 2020, so a bigger wave of easing was layered on top of a bubble that had not yet dissipated — at least one and a half bubbles accumulated today. Central bank governors have learned to print more money immediately when a crisis first appears, and the endogenous result is inflation, rising financial assets and widening wealth inequality all intensifying at once. As long as the bubble is not allowed to clear, the world may face a form of long-term stagflation.

item.title: Central Banks Won't Kill the $100 Bill: It's a $2.5 Trillion Interest-Free Loan
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-oddlots-央行不愿废除百元美钞-那是一笔-2-5-万亿无息贷款/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-oddlots-央行不愿废除百元美钞-那是一笔-2-5-万亿无息贷款/
item.description: Cash use keeps falling, yet currency in circulation keeps hitting records. Central banks have an incentive to keep printing $100 bills: the money is effectively a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the U.S. government, paid for by making life easier for money launderers worldwide.
item.content:encoded:
Cash use keeps falling, yet currency in circulation keeps hitting records. Central banks have an incentive to keep printing $100 bills: the money is effectively a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the U.S. government, paid for by making life easier for money launderers worldwide.

It strips money laundering back from "bank wires" to watches, tractors, casino chips and VAT loopholes, and explains why central banks can't bear to kill the $100 bill.

5:09 The scale of money laundering hasn't moved in thirty years
The most commonly used estimate of money laundering is 2% to 5% of global GDP a year, which at today's roughly $100 trillion GDP is $2 trillion to $5 trillion. That figure traces back to a rough estimate by former IMF managing director Michel Camdessus in the late 1990s, and nobody has come up with a better answer since. Oliver warns that the more alarming fact is that the ratio hasn't changed in thirty years: decades of anti-money-laundering action have not shrunk the criminal economy, only barely held it from growing faster than the overall economy.

9:10 Banks spend $200 billion a year on AML and get close to nothing
When banks complain that KYC is too expensive, it isn't just whining. The U.S. passed the Bank Secrecy Act in 1970, and in 1989 the FATF pushed anti-money-laundering out as a global norm, forcing banks to hire compliance teams and install AI monitoring software. LexisNexis estimates global AML compliance costs about $200 billion a year — enough to solve world hunger and give everyone clean water. Yet the system generates a huge volume of suspicious activity reports every year, and launderers still run ahead of regulators. The problem isn't that banks aren't trying; it's that the whole system is expensive, weakly feedback-driven, and almost nobody is accountable for outcomes.

12:14 Trade-based laundering is an order of magnitude bigger than cash smuggling
Cash smuggling makes laundering inside the banking system look small, but the bigger chunk never touches money at all: value is hidden inside goods. Roughly $25 billion in cash flows into Mexico each year, while John Deere and Caterpillar farm equipment exported from the U.S. becomes the consideration cartels get back; European luxury goods flow to China, drugs and goods flow back the other way, and the triangle is settled with misinvoiced paperwork. Global Financial Integrity estimates this kind of trade-based laundering at about $1 trillion a year. A million-dollar watch on your wrist through customs is far easier than moving a million in cash.

17:18 The Vancouver model: Chinese cash demand meets cartel supply
China caps currency exchange at $50,000 per person per year, yet wealthy Chinese have plenty of demand to spend abroad. The Vancouver model matches that demand with the dollar cash supply from drug cartels: bags of cash outside Canadian casinos go to Chinese gamblers, the money is lost at the tables, and the gamblers run up gambling debts; that debt is offset on the other end in China by an RMB transaction and the drug sales that follow. Looked at as a single gambling session it looks like a loss; looked at across the whole chain, it is a triangular settlement that simultaneously repatriates cartel money and moves Chinese capital out. The model later spread worldwide, with luxury goods, consumer goods and drugs all serving as vehicles for moving value.

23:25 A VAT loophole lets the same goods extract 20% over and over
Zero-rated cross-border transactions in the EU were meant to keep national tax authorities from having to audit each other, but they became an ATM: goods entering the UK from Ireland owe no VAT, and when sold to an affiliated shell company 20% is added; that shell company re-exports the goods back to Ireland and claims a refund from UK tax authorities for the 20% it never paid. Round and round it goes, hence carousel fraud. The UK once largely suppressed it with a multi-agency crackdown, and the fraudsters then moved to continental Europe, where it now runs about €50 billion a year, spreading from Lithuania all the way to Portugal. Criminal organizations have no ceiling on cooperation: the more they cooperate, the bigger they get.

27:27 Nobody uses cash, yet central banks are printing record amounts of it
In the digital-payment era, cash is down to about 9% of transactions in the UK and about 13% in the U.S., so by ordinary logic the supply of paper money should be shrinking. After Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey raised the banknote paradox in 2009, the phenomenon only intensified: the value of UK notes in circulation doubled, and U.S. currency approached $2.5 trillion. Central banks blaming it on "store of value" doesn't hold up — surveys show the average American adult carries only a bit over $400, while per-capita U.S. currency in circulation works out to more than $7,000. The Fed estimates about 65% of U.S. bills are abroad, but that only pushes the question past the border: nobody knows whose hands these notes are actually sitting in.

32:31 The $100 bill is a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the government
Seigniorage can't simply be understood as the profit from printing money: a $100 bill costs 9 cents, but it isn't "sold" to you — you can always exchange it back for goods at face value, so cash held by the public is essentially an interest-free loan. With close to $2.5 trillion of U.S. currency in circulation, the U.S. government gets interest-free funding equal to about 6% of the national debt; federal interest payments are now about 19% of the budget, and if that $2.5 trillion also had to pay interest, you'd add roughly another percentage point. That is exactly why central banks don't want to hear anyone discuss abolishing cash.

47:51 AML incentives are inverted: the more reports, the less crime gets policed
Suspicious activity reports were meant to be real-time intelligence for law enforcement, but reality is the exact opposite: banks hire thousands of compliance officers to fill out reports, law enforcement has no resources to read them, and most reports fall into a black hole; a bank that misses one can face billion-dollar fines, while getting it right earns no reward. A side effect is debanking — large numbers of people who come under suspicion, many of them Muslim, get cut off by financial institutions. The guest's fix isn't hiring more compliance officers but generating fewer reports, actually reading them, and genuinely prosecuting financial criminals — raising the cost of laundering instead of drowning everyone in paperwork.

item.title: Russia Is Stuck in Ukraine, but It Still Has Room to Open a New Front Against NATO
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-hiddenforces-俄罗斯陷在乌克兰-仍有余力对北约开新战线/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-hiddenforces-俄罗斯陷在乌克兰-仍有余力对北约开新战线/
item.description: Russia has not won in Ukraine, but attrition has forged the world's most advanced drone-infantry warfare experience; the guest argues it has ample capacity to mount a limited probe against NATO, and the window is in the final phase of Trump's term.
item.content:encoded:
Russia has not won in Ukraine, but attrition has forged the world's most advanced drone-infantry warfare experience; the guest argues it has ample capacity to mount a limited probe against NATO, and the window is in the final phase of Trump's term.

The guest is the Wall Street Journal's chief diplomatic correspondent and was in Kyiv on the day of the 2022 invasion; his judgments on Russian military capability and Europe's fractures are far more concrete than those of TV commentators.

19:16 Trump's anti-Europe talk may be taken literally by Putin
Everyone is speculating about whether John Ratcliffe's secret trip to Russia was there to negotiate terms. The guest's judgment is that the visit looks more like carrying a message to Moscow on Trump's behalf: don't take those on-air remarks about America not caring about Europe seriously — if Russia invades Lithuania, Estonia or Finland, the US will send troops. The reasoning is that Moscow is bogged down in an attritional war in Ukraine and badly needs to cut off European support for Kyiv, so escalating with a probe against NATO is one option, and Trump's earlier statements that Europe is a bunch of freeloaders gave Putin room to misread, hence the need for a dedicated trip to make the red line clear. One caveat: the guest does not have intelligence from inside that room; he is explaining why the account is entirely plausible, not confirming it.

21:27 Russia's army isn't broken and can still open a limited front
Russia has been unable to take Ukraine for a long time — does that mean it cannot open another front? The guest's answer is blunt: it can absolutely open a limited front — not tanks rolling across Poland all the way to Paris, but action in the Baltic direction, such as sealing off the narrow land corridor of the Suwalki Gap. He says the Russian and Ukrainian armies are the only two in the world today that fight modern drone-infantry warfare as a daily routine. The story of a 20-person Ukrainian drone team destroying an entire traditional battalion is widely told, but the Russian military has the same technology in hand: 20 Russians can likewise wipe out a NATO battalion that has not trained against drones. Outsiders assume Russia grows weaker the longer it fights, and overlook that it is also one of the parties tempered by this technological revolution.

22:31 NATO might not even rescue Lithuania from Poland
A war game designed to simulate a Russian invasion of Lithuania led the guest to a deeply unsettling conclusion: even Poland did not send troops to save Lithuania, let alone other allies. The reason is not a lack of military capability but the speed of Russian advance, combined with the shadow of nuclear deterrence, which would leave allies caught in hesitation over whether to enter, producing a chain of waiting and watching. The guest says Moscow factors exactly this into its options. He also cautions that this is different from before 2022 — back then, hundreds of thousands of Russian troops massing could be clearly seen on the German and Belarusian borders, and no such material preparation exists now. So the most immediate escalation may not be a conventional invasion but small, ambiguous attacks that can be denied (hitting warehouses or drones first).

23:40 Russia is already probing NATO's limits with drones
At this stage, with no sign of a massed army on the border, Russia still holds a set of low-cost, low-attribution options: a limited strike on a NATO warehouse near Poland or Romania, or a provocation using a captured Ukrainian drone that has been modified, then watching whether NATO splits and whether the US steps in. The guest points out that such probing is already underway — an armed drone attacked a Ukrainian aircraft parked at Leipzig airport in Germany, and only a drone malfunction prevented fatalities; Russian risk-taking is steadily rising, and the West has so far given no serious response. The senior European officers he speaks with all believe the most dangerous window is the next one to two years, roughly falling in the final phase of Trump's term — the Kremlin will want to act before the US might let go.

27:53 Putin wants Ukraine disarmed, not a ceasefire
Would Putin accept an honorable ceasefire deal? The guest's view is that you only need to look at what is put on the table: Russia has consistently demanded not just territory but a cap on the size of Ukraine's army, limits on weapons types, and a cutoff of Western military aid to Ukraine. In his words, the goal is to leave Ukraine unable to defend itself; not neutral, but emasculated, so it cannot rise again in the next phase of the war — a year, five years or ten years later. Putin signed Minsk-1 and Minsk-2, and violated both. So the guest quotes the summary of Ukraine's former foreign minister: this war will end in one of only two ways — the end of Ukraine, or the end of the Russian imperial project. Waiting for the other side to change its mind is not an option.

31:08 Street protests can decide the fate of a wartime cabinet
Kyiv's recent personnel earthquake looks on the surface like an anti-corruption storm, but the key mechanism lies elsewhere: elections are frozen in wartime, and the president's legitimacy rests on street support as its only ballast. Zelensky initially fired Defense Minister Fedorov, who drove drone innovation, because he needed the backing of Commander-in-Chief Syrsky; after Fedorov was dismissed, Kyiv's elites took to the streets, and the protests, small as they were, were enough to make the president reverse course — he removed Syrsky, brought in a younger general more popular at the front, and appointed a defense minister with a veteran intelligence background acceptable to all sides. Ukraine's independent anti-corruption bodies can still pursue people in the president's innermost circle, and when Zelensky tried to amend the law to bring that body under his control, he backed down within a week under street pressure. When elections are absent, the square equals the ballot box.

38:37 Resistance comes from memory, not heroism
Summing up Ukrainian perseverance as patriotic heroism misses what actually drives them. The guest says that after Russian troops take a Ukrainian town, one of the first things they often do is bring in bulldozers to tear down monuments to the victims of the 1930s famine — what they want to erase is a memory. Russian state television talks about how to re-educate Ukrainians, to make them forget their language and culture and become Russians. Around World War II, the Soviets carried out a systematic purge of Ukraine's cultural elite, and in the guest's childhood he had no idea those writers existed, because collective memory had been wiped out. Ukrainians today are almost all descendants of survivors of that meat grinder, carrying the trauma in their bodies; it is the fear of never again that makes them prefer to die on the battlefield rather than return to that life.

45:59 Half a million veterans blocked the first wave of collapse
On the night of February 23, 2022, most people in Kyiv still did not believe there would be a war; the guest remembers knowing from his experience in Kabul and Baghdad that impossible can flip overnight, but ordinary Ukrainians had no such reference point. What really kept the country from collapsing in the first days was eight years of war in the Donbas: that fighting was far from Kyiv, but it produced roughly 500,000 Ukrainians who had traded fire with the Russian army, and volunteer organizations evolved into a flexible, aggressive force. The psychological threshold had already been crossed in the Donbas — we know what they look like, we know how to fight them. Because of that experience, the swift collapse Putin expected did not happen, and the West's widespread expectations were wrong too.

item.title: A Child Who Hits, Bites, or Kicks Isn't Misbehaving — He's Reclaiming Bodily Autonomy
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-parentmojo-孩子打咬踢不是坏行为-是在夺回身体自主权/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-parentmojo-孩子打咬踢不是坏行为-是在夺回身体自主权/
item.description: Stop asking how to make the hitting stop. For a three- or four-year-old, hitting, biting, and kicking are often the only tool left to shout "I have no say" after adults have taken control of nearly everything his body does — give some choice back, and the behavior shrinks.
item.content:encoded:
Stop asking how to make the hitting stop. For a three- or four-year-old, hitting, biting, and kicking are often the only tool left to shout "I have no say" after adults have taken control of nearly everything his body does — give some choice back, and the behavior shrinks.

Most approaches repeat "no hitting" and add punishment, never touching the need that precedes the behavior. This episode treats aggression as a need signal and demonstrates the scripts and cases for negotiating with teachers.

4:21 A child who hits is shouting that he has no say over his body
Preschool is often the first place a child is controlled in nearly every bodily arrangement by an adult other than his parents: where to sit, how to sit, when to speak and when to move. For the previous three years he could roughly decide when to run and when to use the toilet. Sitting on a rug for 20 minutes without moving is a real deprivation of autonomy; and a three- or four-year-old has no language to assert "my body is mine to decide," so hitting and kicking become one of the few tools still available. So when the incident call comes, don't rush to lecture "hands to yourself." The question to ask is: how much say did this child have over his own life before this, and what little bit of it can be handed back now.

6:42 Kindergarten readiness is really obedience training
Teachers often say a given preschool has a high share of kindergarten-ready children, and the core definition of that readiness is compliance: sit down when the teacher says sit, even mid-task, even when the body is already overloaded. Parents fear that if the child doesn't comply now, he won't get into a good elementary school, college, a good life. But the price the child pays for this definition is learning to suppress the feeling of "what I need right now." Teachers aren't villains either — they too need to feel competent, need the children safe, need to conserve energy, and may even take satisfaction from the power; many entered education precisely to repair their own childhood wounds, yet only know the power-over model of relationship. Only by seeing both sides' situations is there room to negotiate.

9:24 We grant ourselves regulation and deny it to children
If an adult feels overloaded at a party, he arrives early, leaves early, hides in a quiet room, even wears noise-canceling earplugs — we consider this perfectly natural. But turn the camera to a child, and apart from conventions like extended exam time, we immediately worry that "too much accommodation will spoil him, and he won't survive the real world." The truth is that adults grant themselves far more accommodation than they allow children. The source offers a concrete image: an adult stronger than you unceremoniously carries you out of the quiet room back to the center of the loud party — swap in an adult and you instantly see it as a violation of bodily autonomy; when it happens to a child we look right past it.

12:11 The repair point is before the behavior, not the behavior itself
Repeating "hitting is not okay" doesn't work, because that isn't the knowledge the child is missing. You need a different set of questions: what happened in the few seconds before this bite? What happened earlier in the day? Is there a move or a new baby in the child's life? A sensory-overloaded child who gets jostled in line will lose it — so put him at the front, the back, or outside the line; a child who struggles with transitions needs a few minutes' warning. The adult analogy: when your partner snaps at you for no reason at night, it's usually not about that sentence but about the morning argument, the sleep debt, and a chain of stress. If the other person then tossed off "your attitude needs work," you'd blow up too; yet we routinely do only the latter to children.

15:10 Talking to the teacher: don't assign blame, hear what the "no" protects
Telling a teacher "please change what you're doing" almost always hits a wall. The safer opening is to drop judgment and reconstruct the facts: don't look for who's responsible, just ask what actually happened; and include family changes, which are context the teacher can't see. Once you know whether the child's trigger is sensory or autonomy, extend empathy to the three things behind the teacher: competence, the child's safety, and the breather that saves energy. The request must land on a concrete, executable change, like "can he sit on a ball outside the circle." If the teacher refuses, the keyword isn't the refusal but what need that "no" is still protecting, and finding a different approach that satisfies both sides.

16:07 A naptime conflict, cleanly dismantled
Jen's daughter Carys, at three, couldn't nap; the teacher wanted her to lie down, and she was bored and frustrated — her need was to play; the teacher had two needs: state rules required offering nap, and naptime was the teacher's own rest period. The solution they found was to move her mat to a slightly separated corner, where she could quietly play with soft toys that wouldn't roll, and the teacher could see her through the window from the break room. The child kept her right to free play, the teacher kept the rule and her rest, and Jen escaped the no-win incident-call loop. This segment shows that "negotiating by need" isn't empty talk: everyone gives a little, but everyone's core need is held.

17:53 Every method comes down to one question
Compress all of the above into one sentence: stop asking "how do I make the hitting stop," and ask instead "what need is this behavior communicating?" Hitting, biting, and kicking are only surface signals; the real message may be "I need sensory relief" or "I need some say over my own body." Once the need is correctly named, a path to meeting it can be designed; and it is almost always the adult who changes the environment, because changing how the adult shows up is far easier than changing the child.

item.title: The Thai Flood That Wrecked the Hard Disk Drive Industry: The Biggest Factory Fell, the Number Two Took the Throne
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-asianometry-泰国洪水重创硬盘业-最大的厂跌倒-老二捡了王座/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-asianometry-泰国洪水重创硬盘业-最大的厂跌倒-老二捡了王座/
item.description: One flood in Thailand rewrote the hard drive rankings: the largest maker, Western Digital, saw shipments fall 51% quarter-over-quarter, while Seagate fell only 8% and overtook it to take the top spot.
item.content:encoded:
One flood in Thailand rewrote the hard drive rankings: the largest maker, Western Digital, saw shipments fall 51% quarter-over-quarter, while Seagate fell only 8% and overtook it to take the top spot.

What are the risks of geographic concentration in a manufacturing supply chain? This flood provides a complete case study — industrial estate siting, zero inventory, and single points of failure all detonating at once.

6:13 Flood walls gave hard drive makers a false sense of security
The industrial estates were built on river floodplain converted from rice paddies north of Bangkok. For flood protection, developers installed ring levees up to two meters high, secondary wave walls, pumps and drainage systems; the parks quickly grew into small cities with their own housing and shops. But this engineering may have misled everyone. When the real flood season arrived in 2011, seven industrial parks were inundated within two weeks. Research later suspected that it was precisely this seemingly complete infrastructure that created a kind of false confidence — the belief that even if it rained, everything would be fine. In other words, what the manufacturers bought was not safety, but an illusion about risk.

8:24 Reservoir releases were not the culprit; local rainfall was
After the flood, dam managers were blamed for releasing water too late, with criticism centering on favoritism toward farmers and rice-corruption allegations. But the research does not support this attribution. A 2023 simulation ran 17 scenarios swapping the release strategies of two dams, and concluded that even with perfect foresight of subsequent rainfall, the flooded area could have been reduced by at most only 3.68%. Another 2020 study examined hydrological station data along the Chao Phraya River and found that in one low-lying disaster area, less than 30% of the floodwater came from the river, while 73.7% came from local rainfall. In other words, the water mainly fell directly on the disaster zone — reservoir decisions cannot carry the blame.

9:25 Why Seagate stalled even though it wasn't flooded
Seagate's factory in northern Korat was basically fine, but production still stopped — because seven of its top ten suppliers were underwater. The typical case was Japan's Nidec, which makes spindle motors for hard drives and halted production outright after two plants flooded. The hard drive supply chain is interlocking layer by layer: no matter how safe the assembly line, if the motors don't come, the whole line stops. Seagate limited its quarterly shipment decline to 8% by quickly qualifying new suppliers, modifying designs to reduce complexity, and negotiating payment terms with suppliers. In the same year, Western Digital's core plant took on water 1.8 meters deep, and quarterly shipments fell 51%. The difference between the two was not whose building was taller, but whose underlying supply chain could route around the break faster.

12:34 Zero inventory amplified the flood into a global shortage
Before the flood hit, the hard drive industry had just completed a round of consolidation: Western Digital announced in March 2011 that it would acquire Hitachi's hard drive business, and a month later Seagate announced the acquisition of Samsung, barely bringing supply and demand back into balance. Precisely because there was no surplus inventory to draw down, the shock was multiplied. Tom Coughlin estimated that Q4 2011 hard drive demand was about 180 million units, while actual production was only 110 million to 120 million; and the flood happened to hit right in the Christmas shopping season. Retail immediately raised spot prices by 20% to 40%, and a 1TB hard drive at Taipei's Guanghua Market went from NT$1,750 to over NT$3,000. Even Intel admitted in December that Q4 revenue would be about $1 billion lower than expected due to the hard drive shortage. A localized flood, transmitted through zero inventory, thus became a global shortage.

15:41 The water receded, but hard drive prices didn't fall for two years
The water receded, but the shortage did not end quickly. Hard drive supply availability only returned to pre-disaster levels about nine months later; retail prices fell back even more slowly — hard drive prices on Newegg did not drop back to pre-disaster levels until April 2013. Backblaze did the math using its own procurement records: in September 2011 the cost per GB was $0.044, and returning to that level again would take until September 2013. Why is it easy to raise prices but hard to lower them? The author lists several interpretations: the ecosystem recovered more slowly than expected, the two giants' 2011 acquisitions brought additional costs, tablets caused PC hard drive demand to permanently decline, and a more cynical guess — after Seagate and Western Digital acquired their second-tier rivals, only three major manufacturers remained in the entire industry, making prices easier to ‘stabilize’, or in his own word: cartelize. As for which one is the truth, he does not conclude.

18:47 The flooded giant chose to stay and keep building walls
Western Digital's post-disaster choice is telling: it did not retreat, but doubled down on defenses. WD and the Bang Pa-in estate owner built an 11-kilometer flood wall along the estate, and WD added a 6-meter-high inner wall around its factory; to add redundancy to its supply chain, in December 2011 it announced a new slider fab in Malaysia. A survey of 50 directly affected Japanese companies showed that nearly 80% decided to stay in Thailand. The reasons are not hard to understand: ready-made estates, supporting infrastructure and skilled workers are hard to pack up and take away. Thailand has since suffered multiple rounds of major flooding, especially in the 2020s when it happened almost every year; in November of the most recent year it even rained in what was billed as a ‘once-in-300-years’ event, but these estates have held out so far. Whether stronger defenses will be needed in the future can only be tested by the next major flood.

item.title: AI designs viruses that infect bacteria, but only 5% of the time
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-twiv-ai-设计出能感染细菌的病毒-但成功率仅-5/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-twiv-ai-设计出能感染细菌的病毒-但成功率仅-5/
item.description: For the first time, AI designed a complete viral genome from scratch that can infect bacteria; experimental validation puts the success rate at about 5%, nowhere near as omnipotent as the media suggests.
item.content:encoded:
For the first time, AI designed a complete viral genome from scratch that can infect bacteria; experimental validation puts the success rate at about 5%, nowhere near as omnipotent as the media suggests.

This episode takes apart the success rate of AI-made viruses, compensatory mutations and biosafety rhetoric, and also demonstrates how an observational vaccine study can be falsified by an E-value.

12:43 A vaccine switch as a natural control
The trap in "healthy vaccinee bias" is that vaccinated people tend to pay more attention to their own health than unvaccinated people, so comparing the two groups mistakes lifestyle differences for vaccine effects. This study exploits the moment in 2017 when the US shingles vaccine switched wholesale from Zostavax to Shingrix: before the policy switch people received the old vaccine, after it they received the new one, and both groups were people who actively sought vaccination, so in theory the bias is erased. It is still not a randomised trial, however — unmeasured factors such as socioeconomic status, smoking and diet could still be unbalanced between the two groups, so it counts only as a quasi-experiment.

15:47 Weak confounding alone can overturn a vaccine benefit
How strong would unmeasured confounding have to be to overturn an observational conclusion? Measure it with the E-value. The E-value for this vaccine study is only 1.42, almost hugging 1, meaning a not-particularly-strong confounder associated with both "which vaccine was received" and "cardiovascular outcome" could explain away the observed risk reduction. An E-value needs to reach 3.4 or even 5 for a conclusion to count as solid; 1.42 is far from robust. The authors themselves concede that a randomised clinical trial is needed to confirm it, and that this observation cannot be treated as evidence.

38:13 AI produces a functional viral genome for the first time
The researchers took the genomic language models EVO1 and EVO2 and had them write phage genomes: first the models read massive public DNA sequence datasets, then they were fine-tuned on PhiX174 to generate thousands of candidate sequences. Back in the lab, only about 5% of the products could actually infect E. coli — the first time AI has designed a complete genome from scratch and had it proven functional. If the media summarises this as "AI directly made a virus", it misses a key point: the model has only ever seen sequences, with no experimental annotation telling it which base does what, and the 5% hit rate shows how ignorant it still is about how sequence determines function.

44:37 The origin of replication is the model's most conserved memory
The prompt given to the model needed only the first 4 to 9 nucleotides of the PhiX174 genome for the accuracy of the output to rise markedly. The authors found that this unremarkable stretch is part of the origin of replication, and it was 100% conserved across every genome the model generated. It works like a password meaning "I am a real virus": the model treats the origin of replication as a core that must be locked down, and only dares to let other positions evolve. This also explains why such a short prompt works — what matters is not the prompt's length but whether it hits a functional pressure point.

56:55 Swap one gene and AI adds 58 mutations itself
The design idea behind EVO36 was not to rewrite the whole genome but to swap genes: replace PhiX174's J gene with the shorter J protein from phage G4. When humans performed the same transplant by hand in the past, the product could not infect; but the AI-produced EVO36 infects normally, because it accumulated an extra 58 mutations across the genome. These look like compensatory mutations that let the foreign J protein re-adapt to its local environment. Humans might not think to touch 58 positions at once, and this is exactly where generative models exceed the capability of single-point editing.

1:00:15 A mixed phage cocktail takes on resistant bacteria
Natural PhiX174 runs into a wall against already-resistant bacteria and cannot break through even after five passages; 16 AI-synthesised phages mixed together infected the previously resistant strain within one or two generations. Resistance is not broken by any single phage but by several synthetic phages recombining with each other and accumulating new mutations during replication, finally breaking the barrier through collective action. The result suggests that phage therapy should bet not on a single strain but on a cocktail of multiple synthetic phages.

1:07:29 Don't call AI-made viruses an urgent threat
For that study generating PhiX174, a contemporaneous commentary used the word "urgent" to describe its biosafety implications. Vincent pushed back on that wording directly on the show: the authors had already shown through reproducible experiments that this kind of research can be done safely, so what is needed is not an alarm bell but the start of building safety frameworks. He also stressed that reconstructing viruses is not science fiction as long as you have enough sequence — which is precisely why frameworks are needed rather than fearmongering.

1:35:53 Not getting vaccinated is often just not knowing
Discussing the unvaccinated population, the article raises an often overlooked mechanism: some people do not get vaccinated not out of religious or ideological opposition but because they simply do not know they should. Treating vaccine hesitancy uniformly as a "matter of belief" misdirects policy — for this group the key is not debate or persuasion but information outreach so they first learn the vaccine exists.

item.title: Sports Betting Has Infiltrated Gen Z, and the Regulatory Risk Is Underestimated
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-excessreturns-体育博彩渗透z世代-金融监管风险被低估/
