item.description: Most people assume it's wealth ambition that carries founders through. Paul Graham says what actually pushes people forward day to day is disaster fear — the server going down, the model train about to fall off the table. You keep your head down for ten years, look up, do the math on the last round's valuation, and realize you're already a billionaire.
item.content:encoded:
Most people assume it's wealth ambition that carries founders through. Paul Graham says what actually pushes people forward day to day is disaster fear — the server going down, the model train about to fall off the table. You keep your head down for ten years, look up, do the math on the last round's valuation, and realize you're already a billionaire.

After 21 years and 47 batches, PG's judgment: AI has changed almost nothing about startups — only the bill. Useful for calibrating your confidence that "this time is different."

2:02 People nostalgic for the golden age forget the only hit back then was Reddit
Since roughly 2008, people have been saying YC is finished — PG's read is that its attackers have to first admit it was once good, so they can only ever say "not what it used to be." But his counterexample is concrete: the flagship of the supposed good old days was Reddit, whereas the projects he did office hours with this batch include an intercontinental ballistic freight company — like an ICBM, except it doesn't explode on landing, it unloads. Another category is curing cancer. He says there are too many ways to go at it — vaccines at one end, therapies at the other — so you should fund several, and any one that works is worth it. This batch has a company doing on-demand research for cancer patients, and what he likes is exactly that approach: cancer is famously not something you beat by "coming up with a cure" — maybe the way to beat it is death by a thousand cuts.

4:09 Google won't be breached, it will be rendered obsolete by the world
Many of the ideas in the 2012 "frighteningly ambitious" list have already been done, and one of them was "the new Google." PG says he predicted the path back then: you can't attack Google head-on, you can only wait for the day the world changes enough that its model goes stale. OpenAI is that change itself — after using it, he found he no longer uses search, because what he always wanted wasn't web pages, it was information, so he just asks the AI. This is a corollary that holds for every incumbent: moats aren't breached, they're rendered obsolete.

6:15 Ambition is the ticket in; the daily fuel is fear of looking like a fool
Ambition is a necessity, because the obstacles in startups are too terrifying to push through on conscientiousness alone. But PG says what actually gets a founder moving at any given moment isn't "if I solve this I'll become a billionaire" — it's disaster fear: the server is down, the fear of looking like an idiot. His image is a toy train — the engine is just going over the edge of the table and you lunge to catch it. You keep your head down fixing that train for ten years, look up, do the math on the last round's valuation, and realize you're already a billionaire. He says sometimes he's the one who does the math first and tells the founder.

9:21 The only test of formidable is whether they get what they want
Formidable is a private word PG and Jessica were using before YC. His definition is operational: this person gets what they want in any situation — if they can't, what are we even talking about. That definition incidentally explains the investing logic: you hold stock in his company, he holds it too, interests are aligned; he gets what he wants, you get what you want. It's also the precondition for his answer to "where does the next trillion-dollar company come from."

11:24 Lean startup isn't dead: even rocket companies can start on little money
Asked whether lean startup is dead and whether you now have to burn big money from day one, PG's rebuttal has two layers. First, price: tokens are expensive now only because of the GPU shortage; the price for the same level of inference will fall by roughly 30x a year, and on top of that you're getting higher-quality tokens — technology always gets cheaper. Second, path: even rocket companies can start on not much money; you can't build a real rocket, but you can build the design, run simulations, show it to experts, and if it's convincing enough you get the next round. StarCloud wrote a white paper and booked a launch — though he adds that that founder is himself a well-known expert in the field with built-in credibility; a fresh graduate doesn't have it that easy.

13:24 AI went the wrong direction: from human toward perfect
People doing AI in the 1980s thought the path started from "the perfect fly": able to do only what a fly does, but as well as a fly does it; then climb up to mouse, cat, monkey, human, each level perfect. What we got was the reverse — a complete human right out of the gate, just talking nonsense, like an undergrad trying to bluff his way through a paper. What got optimized was the opposite dimension: not from perfect toward human, but from human toward perfect. That also explains the jagged frontier: it can solve hard math problems but can't tell you what time a restaurant opens.

16:30 AI changed the bill structure, not the shipping speed
PG says the best predictor of startup success is still shipping speed, and AI hasn't replaced that metric — with these tools in hand, plenty of companies in this batch still don't ship fast enough, which shows the difference isn't how fast you can write things; you first have to come up with the ideas. "With AI, what's still unchanged?" His answer: so far almost everything is exactly the same. The only strange new thing is the bill structure — the biggest cost of a startup used to be salaries, everything else was cheap by comparison; now there's GPU on top, and tokens can burn tens of thousands of dollars a day.

19:36 The next trillion-dollar company comes from the right person, not the right idea
Asked where the next trillion-dollar company will come from, PG swaps the question from sector to person outright: it comes from the right founder, not some particular idea — startup ideas are highly variable, and he'll only concede "probably not dog-walking." Conversely, to judge whether a company is worth investing in, first judge whether the founder is formidable; what they're working on is probably promising. As for whether future founders will look different, he says there are already 20 years of data: today's founders are exactly the same as 20 years ago, and there's no reason the next 20 will be different.

item.title: Arm Moves Into Building CPUs: The Biggest Bottleneck in Chip Design Is Verification, Not Design
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-nopriors-arm-下场造-cpu-芯片设计最大瓶颈是验证-不是设计/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-nopriors-arm-下场造-cpu-芯片设计最大瓶颈是验证-不是设计/
item.description: The real time sink in a chip cycle is verification, debug and documentation, not RTL; 80%-90% of Arm engineers already use AI daily, and Arm is breaking its 98.5%-margin licensing model to build CPUs itself.
item.content:encoded:
The real time sink in a chip cycle is verification, debug and documentation, not RTL; 80%-90% of Arm engineers already use AI daily, and Arm is breaking its 98.5%-margin licensing model to build CPUs itself.

It uses real internal Arm data to explain what AI is actually good for in chip design, then strings product, capital and supply-chain judgments into one closed loop — worth checking against your own expectations if you work in AI infrastructure.

3:43 Arm is building CPUs itself because customers are pushing it to
Arm used to sell only IP licenses at 98.5% gross margin, never touching inventory or wafers. One step forward, the compute subsystem already had customers grabbing pre-assembled CPU, GPU and memory "subsystems" as modules. The next step came because "customers who want a general-purpose CPU for the large-model era can't find a supplier" and went straight to Arm to push for one. Before announcing, Arm asked nearly every license customer, and opposition was minimal: a bigger software ecosystem benefits every customer, so Nvidia, Amazon, Microsoft and Google — all companies building Arm server chips — publicly supported it.

8:07 Banning AI tools is sending engineers back to the library
A full chip design cycle is 24-36 months; the biggest time sink is not RTL generation or architecture mapping but verification, validation, debug and documentation. AI is especially well suited to those steps, and roughly 80%-90% of Arm engineers already use AI daily; turning the tools off would be like telling people in the 1990s they could use the internet only two hours a day and had to go back downstairs to the library for the rest. What AI is weakest at today is RTL generation and physical design, because models depend on public corpora while the industry's most critical details are private data — exactly the gap companies like Arm can fill.

10:35 From idea to layout is a five-year wait, not two or three
The host asked: once AI eats verification, the most time-consuming step, can 24-36 months shrink to 6-12? Rene Haas gave a measured answer: 2-3 years is unrealistic; five years or more, for designs with not-too-complex constraints, going from idea all the way to GDSII (the layout file handed to the fab) is possible. If you type into the tool "make a chip 10% faster, 20% cheaper and 30% more power-efficient than some reference," don't expect one click. His judgment is that in 5-10 years the whole industry's design methodology will change markedly.

15:00 AI supply and demand are still far apart, and the bottleneck is the construction site, not the wafer
On the AI bubble, Rene Haas says you have to separate valuation froth at the stock level from the industry chain itself; he states plainly that supply versus demand is still "far apart." Transformer inference and training eat both compute and memory, and demand won't stop. The real hard constraint will move to data center construction: many projects are running late and need more hands, and resistance limiting new data center builds is appearing in various places; over the next 3-5 years the constraint may not be wafer capacity or memory but the physical build-out staying perpetually tight.

17:14 SoftBank doing cloud is about being a customer for chip companies
For chip/AI founders with heavy assets and heavy capex: capital availability is itself the gate, and strategic partnerships need to reach early into all three layers — supply chain, PE and banks. Behind Arm is SoftBank, and not just as a shareholder; SoftBank has just announced it will build a "neo cloud"-style service, which lets young chip companies avoid lining up only at Microsoft's or Google's door for a design win and instead form a direct customer relationship with the Arm/SoftBank ecosystem — one more path to deployment.

21:25 Humanoids won't unify everything; specialized robots will coexist long-term
Rene Haas sees robot 1.0 as purpose-built: mechanics and software both optimized for a single motion, and switching a production line means nearly starting over. A new generation of robots that can redefine tasks through training, with mechanical bodies that are also general-purpose, will first eat repetitive labor in construction, infrastructure and security. Form factor won't go in a single direction: factories, warehouses and tools are all designed to human dimensions, so humanoids have an edge; another set of tasks suits specialized forms better. Cost has to come down first, and delivery and warehousing will be the earliest automated scenarios.

27:13 Restricting chips to China is an unwinnable infinite game
On US manufacturing he is direct: the US should build more fabs at home, needed both for national security and for supply-chain diversification. On export controls, he frames it as an "infinite game" — restricting chips to China cannot produce a victory with an end state, and may instead push key technology out of the US. He also rejects the idea that data centers are "big warehouses with no jobs": energy, liquid cooling and the surrounding ecosystem are all jobs that can be created in the US.

36:00 In a token world, every path runs through a CPU
If you use the token factory metaphor for accelerators, Rene Haas thinks the real system question is: who orchestrates and arbitrates where those tokens go, and delivers them to users. He believes every path runs through a CPU: beyond training, there is inference scheduling, system orchestration, context and tool calls. At the edge, on devices that can't carry a 50W GPU, Arm's power advantage is even more obvious. The CPU hasn't disappeared; it has formed persistent demand alongside accelerators.

item.title: The Number One Fraud Red Flag Isn't Greed — It's a Personal Financial Breakdown
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-rationalreminder-金融舞弊头号预警-不是贪婪-是个人财务先失控/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-rationalreminder-金融舞弊头号预警-不是贪婪-是个人财务先失控/
item.description: For 14 consecutive years, ACFE has ranked "personal financial problems" as the top red flag for financial misconduct; systemic incentives, a deactivated critical brain region and moral overconfidence all let good people cross the line step by step.
item.content:encoded:
For 14 consecutive years, ACFE has ranked "personal financial problems" as the top red flag for financial misconduct; systemic incentives, a deactivated critical brain region and moral overconfidence all let good people cross the line step by step.

One author is a clinical neuropsychologist, the other has 20 years of experience suing financial advisers; the offender profiles and warning signals here have more screening value than moral slogans.

2:04 The test for crossing the line is one sentence: this is not your money
Moira defines financial misconduct as "doing bad things with other people's money": it includes both taking money for yourself and guiding or advising others to use funds in ways that aren't in their best interest. She stresses that anyone working in finance must always remember "this is not your money." Reducing the ethical problem to fiduciary duty gives all the later red flags a single baseline for judgment.

9:10 For 14 straight years, the top red flag is personal financial problems
Philippa cites ACFE's global report: for 14 consecutive years, the number one fraud red flag has not been greed but "personal financial problems" — people whose personal finances are out of control, who can't make ends meet or are drowning in debt, are the most likely to get involved in financial misconduct. The financial industry offers access to other people's money and attracts people who chase wealth, and people are irrational about money on top of that; the three conditions stack into fertile ground for misconduct.

13:14 Listening to advice, the brain acts like it's praying: the critical region goes offline
Moira notes that neuroimaging evidence shows that when people receive financial advice, key critical regions of the brain "go offline," in a state similar to the brain during prayer. People feel safe, trusting and open, and this non-critical state heightens vulnerability, especially for those unfamiliar with finance. She gives the example that even hedge fund managers will "sit and wait for answers" in front of an adviser rather than asking how the product actually works.

19:19 Good people start erring through obedience and eagerness to help, not greed
Philippa and Moira break down the path by which good people go wrong: blindly obeying orders, crossing lines out of "misguided helpfulness," hiding the mistake out of fear, then covering it with a bigger lie. "John" in the book slides from a small slip into lying, then into doubling down on the cover-up. Moira stresses that ethics is not a solo sport but a team sport; if the organizational culture tacitly permits misconduct, it's very hard for an individual to stay clean.

37:36 Psychopaths flow into finance disproportionately
Responding to Cameron's concern, Moira says the evidence shows psychopaths flow disproportionately into finance and business because "that's where the money is." She cites Robert Hare's research: successful psychopaths tend to be charming and are extremely good at spotting and exploiting other people's desires. The damage they do is large, and they often keep circulating within the industry because colleagues feel a "sense of relief," leaving the problem for the next firm.

53:50 Most people don't realize they're making an ethical decision at all
Traditional ethics training always presents clear moral dilemmas in the classroom, but real-world problems tend to emerge quietly, so people don't realize they're at a fork in the road. Moira cites Kahneman's "what you see is all there is": people don't question the motives of product providers, don't think about who benefits from a complex product, and don't admit they haven't actually understood it. The result is that even with ethics training, most of the time they don't know they're facing an ethical decision.

1:02:56 The future wrongdoer is a vulnerable ordinary person, not a bad guy
Philippa lists the profile of the future wrongdoer: early in their career (Evan got pulled into a global fraud one month after joining and was banned for life nine months later), in debt, highly dependent on their boss, a people-pleaser, low self-esteem (compensated for with a luxury car), fatigued, family problems and so on. These signals are rarely used by the industry to screen advisers for their own biases; they aren't some rare evil but the shared weaknesses of ordinary people under pressure and vulnerability.

1:09:07 After 20 years of suing, she has never sued a single CFP holder
Philippa practiced law for 20 years and sued many financial professionals, but never once sued any CFP holder. She believes there's no simple way to pick out a good adviser, but holding a certification is a positive signal. She also offers a test: if an adviser only talks about investments and doesn't understand the client's whole life situation, that's just wealth management, not financial planning — the subject of planning is the person, not the assets.

item.title: The 5% Treasury Yield Isn't About Inflation: $32 Trillion of Debt Means Buyers Will Only Take More
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-oddlots-美债利率上-5-不是通胀闹的-32-万亿国债让买家只肯加价接盘/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-oddlots-美债利率上-5-不是通胀闹的-32-万亿国债让买家只肯加价接盘/
item.description: Inflation can't explain a 30-year above 5%: even with no inflation and no default risk, a buyer already full up on Treasuries at 5.3% won't budge for another $10 billion. What's really steepening the curve is $2 trillion of new supply a year, and the Treasury can't hold it down with buybacks.
item.content:encoded:
Inflation can't explain a 30-year above 5%: even with no inflation and no default risk, a buyer already full up on Treasuries at 5.3% won't budge for another $10 billion. What's really steepening the curve is $2 trillion of new supply a year, and the Treasury can't hold it down with buybacks.

The mainstream narrative pins the 30-year at 5% on inflation; this episode offers a genuinely additive alternative framework, folding the limits of Treasury intervention, the mechanics of Fed balance-sheet runoff, and the term premium debate into one logic.

4:04 5% is first a Treasury interest bill, not a macro signal
Host Joe asks Daryl what he sees when the 30-year Treasury yield is above 5% — even after it ticked down slightly that day following the Fed chair's remarks. Daryl's answer isn't a macro model but the Treasury's predicament: if I were the Treasury secretary, what I'd see is that US government interest expense is extraordinarily high, and I'd have to find a way to push yields down. That line sets the frame for the whole episode: the official side has a strong motive to hold down long-end rates, but whether it can and whether it should are the premises for everything that follows.

5:07 The Treasury wants to sell another $10 billion, it can only pay more
Daryl gives the episode's central thought experiment: suppose there's no inflation risk and no sovereign default, and you're a macro hedge fund that already holds $20 billion of 10-year Treasuries. The Treasury secretary calls and asks you to buy another $10 billion — why don't you want to? The answer: at a 5.3% yield you've already made the allocation you want, and to get you to add, you'd have to be paid a higher rate to compensate. This logic incidentally explains the structural shift on the demand side — foreign central banks are already full up and no longer buying, so new Treasury supply can only land with domestic free discretionary buyers: banks, pensions, insurers, hedge funds, and that money is highly sensitive to yield.

8:10 The logic didn't change, the debt stock hit a tipping point
Joe raises the objection that has to be faced: aging populations, a political system with no appetite for spending cuts, unsustainable deficits — this bearish logic existed in 2018 and 2019, and Japan was talked about this way for decades before that, so why did yields fall relentlessly then and rise now? Daryl's answer is a scale effect: the 60% debt/GDP red line the IMF drew back then is far behind us, France is already at 100%; the US Treasury market grew from about $18 trillion to $31 trillion and keeps expanding. There's no new logic — the quantity of debt itself has accumulated to a tipping point.

10:13 The long end's 5% is mostly issuance, not inflation expectations
Since the short end is still pinned by high inflation and the Fed, why not attribute the high 30-year yield directly to inflation expectations? Daryl concedes inflation over the past five years has indeed run well above the Fed's target and the job isn't done, but points out that implied inflation expectations backed out of real versus nominal bonds are not flashing alarm; the investors actually buying and selling 10-, 20- and 30-year Treasuries are not processing inflation first in their heads — they're processing supply relative to demand. He mentions John Cochrane's fiscal theory of the price level, but that's a long-run framework — the main driver of today's term premium is issuance, not prices.

13:18 Buybacks to cap yields are just a signal, with far too little ammunition
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced an expansion of Treasury buybacks, with liquidity as the official rationale. Daryl reads the subtext directly: from the wording of his public remarks, he doesn't think the problem is market liquidity, he thinks yields are "too high," and he says outright that he's sending a signal to the market. The problem is that the Treasury's operations are a drop in the bucket relative to the whole Treasury market, and the market moved briefly on the news before reversing fast. Trying to suppress the path of yields with the government's own resources has a precedent — the 1992 sterling crisis — and Bessent was the man shorting the pound at Soros's fund.

19:22 The buyback's real job is sweeping up old bonds, not steering rates
The original design of the buyback program was not to steer yields: as the Treasury keeps issuing new securities, a large stock of illiquid off-the-run old bonds is left in the market, clogging dealer balance sheets and trading away from a smooth yield curve. A paper Daryl is working on with two New York Fed economists tests whether sweeping up the fragments on a "regular, predictable" schedule and swapping in new issues can improve market liquidity and earn taxpayers a buy-low, sell-high return. "Odd lots" happens to be where the show's name comes from. He thinks this routine operation works; the Treasury stepping in at a moment of emergency to defend its own bond market is a different matter.

25:30 The runoff constraint is reserves, not the asset side
A new Fed chair wants to shrink the balance sheet, but most people only watch the asset side. Daryl points to the arithmetic constraint: selling assets requires extinguishing an equal amount of liabilities. Of the three liability blocks, the TGA can't have the Treasury pull its deposits out, circulating cash can't be recalled, and the only thing that can be squeezed is commercial banks' reserves at the Fed. But today's reserves are the "Swiss Army knife of the financial industry": they pay interest at market rates, satisfy liquidity regulation, and are usable for payments at any time, so banks have no incentive to give them up. The ratchet effect Acharya and Rajan laid out at Jackson Hole in 2017 already showed it: every time the Fed expands its balance sheet, banks get addicted to reserves, and shrinking it necessarily causes market volatility.

28:33 The task force will swap duration, not actually shrink the size
Daryl states he has no inside information on the task force, but makes two predictions about the group led by Jeremy Stein: first, the real problem isn't size but composition, and the sensible move is to gradually replace the Fed's long-dated Treasuries with short-dated bills, so that reserve interest expense on the liability side offsets bill interest income on the asset side in the same direction, reducing the hit to the Fed's own P&L from swings in the policy rate; second, keep no mortgage-backed securities on the asset side and let them roll off naturally. His own conclusion is blunter: the Fed doesn't necessarily have to shrink the balance sheet, but it must have the tools in hand to shrink it on its own, or it will be backed into a corner when Congress applies pressure.

item.title: A wallet's profit engine isn't interest on balances, it's money moving inside the system
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-complexsys-钱包的利润密码不是余额利息-是钱在体系内流转/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-complexsys-钱包的利润密码不是余额利息-是钱在体系内流转/
item.description: The core ledger of a wallet: money coming in pays card-network tolls, internal transfers cost almost nothing, and cash-out charges again. It earns the spread on flow, not interest on deposits — PayPal, Cash App and Stripe Link are all betting on this model.
item.content:encoded:
The core ledger of a wallet: money coming in pays card-network tolls, internal transfers cost almost nothing, and cash-out charges again. It earns the spread on flow, not interest on deposits — PayPal, Cash App and Stripe Link are all betting on this model.

It takes the wallet cost structure apart for real: wholesale network pricing under ten cents, while platforms can charge users several times that; Japanese players even open accounts at multiple banks to route around clearing. Useful as a business teardown even if you don't do payments.

1:05 A wallet has to answer on day one how it makes money
It opens with the author's own $100 Venmo bill to a barber: for a small transaction that already has a mature payment rail, why does PayPal still want to insert itself in the middle and monetize it. Then it quickly defines the scope: this episode is about the e-wallet business, not crypto private-key wallets; a wallet that appears to hold and disburse balances immediately enters the regulatory zone that treats deposits as sensitive, so from the first day of design a wallet has to answer how it makes money — fail that, and the product dies.

5:14 Card fraud isn't scammers building sites, it's leakage at the issuer
The biggest early obstacle to online transactions was that users didn't dare hand over their card numbers, and the media kept amplifying the risk of card fraud. The author points out the facts are the opposite: most fraud comes from massive data leaks at the issuer end, not from scammers parasitizing websites, and the conclusion is that "economies of scale protect criminals too." PayPal's value was standing between the user's card number and the recipient, capping the risk of a single transaction — which gave it grounds to charge a toll near 3%, and also planted the seed for the balance design that followed.

6:19 A free wallet is not free at all for the wallet itself
Putting money into a wallet goes through the card networks, at a historical list price of about 3%, and that cost is borne by the wallet; but once the balance stays inside the system, transfers between users amount to changing a row in a database, too cheap to bill for. PayPal charges close to full price on both the in and out ends, so simply having "internal transfers replace external ones" adds a chunk of gross margin. A wallet that is free to the average user is not free to the wallet — the zero marginal cost of the float is the real dam.

9:21 Driving down network tolls makes more money than product innovation
There is no necessary relationship between wholesale and retail: buying millions of ACH transactions costs about $0.05 each, while a payment provider can quote merchants close to $0.30; the difference is the tax the platform levies on the underlying plumbing. Japan is more extreme: interbank transfers cost about 200 yen per transaction while intra-bank entries are nearly free, so some products open accounts at each of the top banks, let users' money move inside the banks, and settle through daily netting. In finance, driving down network tolls converts into wallet profit more directly than product innovation.

12:27 Cash-out isn't a user perk, it's a second toll pipe
Cash App prices cash-out the same way: want it fast, pick the more expensive card rail, charged at 1.75% with a 25-cent minimum; the author tested withdrawing $50 and was quoted 88 cents. Paired with that is issuing prepaid cards through partners like Sutton Bank, so money spent outside the system still captures swipe fees. The wallet no longer treats cash-out as a user perk but as a second revenue pipe, because the partner bank needs the wallet's user scale and the wallet needs the bank's issuing license.

20:53 On co-brand cards the wallet takes a cut and carries the bad debt
The logic of a wallet partnering to issue credit cards is charging on both sides, but risk control is the real battlefield: wallets typically assume their accumulated spending data lets them underwrite more accurately than the issuing bank. The industry has repeatedly shown that FICO is already strong enough to be hard to replace; the extra variables that could materially improve losses often cross legal red lines. What actually prices the wallet is the agreement — the bank requires the loss rate on the whole loan portfolio to stay under a threshold, otherwise the wallet's revenue share goes to zero or it even pays in. The 10-K language dances around "loss sharing," but in essence the wallet is carrying the issuer's bad debt.

24:50 Users care about the phone, not the plastic card
Apple's core argument when negotiating with banks is that users care about the phone, not the plastic credit card; if banks won't pay, Apple can also back or build a new two-sided payment network and take users with it. The reported figure is that Apple takes 15 basis points per Apple Pay transaction, while Google reportedly takes nothing — which the author uses to mock the two giants' differing ability to do non-core products. The next layer is the conclusion that the checkout counter itself can be like ad inventory: once the goods and prices are fixed, who gets to rank a payment method first becomes a bidding position, and Stripe has already turned the traditional display into dynamic ordering by user preference, even opening up merchant fine-tuning options.

31:13 Network tolls don't fall at the negotiating table, they fall in the default setting
Extend Link into a general-ledger-level settlement negotiation layer: if users store their low-cost payment methods in Link, the next checkout can bypass the card networks and go through bank accounts; the tolls saved get redistributed between merchants and users. This can't be negotiated by one company sitting at one table — it's the aggregation of decisions by millions of users and merchants, ultimately making the side it represents at the payments negotiating table approach 1% of global GDP. Only that kind of volume earns the right to reprice network tolls.

item.title: If It Can't Solve Quantum Gravity, It Isn't Real AGI
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-spc-解不出量子引力-就不算真正的-agi/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-spc-解不出量子引力-就不算真正的-agi/
item.description: A physicist draws a high line for AGI: solving quantum gravity is what counts. The conversation also clarifies the real relationship between quantum materials and AI — searched-for materials still have to pass the synthesizability gate, and the result may be zero.
item.content:encoded:
A physicist draws a high line for AGI: solving quantum gravity is what counts. The conversation also clarifies the real relationship between quantum materials and AI — searched-for materials still have to pass the synthesizability gate, and the result may be zero.

A noise-reduction pass on the AI world's default judgments: a string theorist makes the returns of science and the boundaries of AI concrete and verifiable, useful for calibrating your own time expectations in hard tech. The narrative is a bit slow; the substance concentrates in the middle and later sections.

17:28 Learning too much paralyzes you; only naivety dares ask the original questions
The hardest part of going from student to researcher isn't absorbing knowledge, it's posing the original questions that push the boundary of knowledge forward. Gopakumar describes this transition as ‘naivety plus experience’: learn too much and you get paralyzed, so you need to keep a bit of naivety to dare ask the questions that look impossible to even start. The advisor's job is to teach you to break the big problem into small steps you can advance right now, without losing the ultimate goal. His own advisor David Gross was very good at this — by his account, Gross's first student produced work that won the Nobel Prize for both student and advisor, and Witten also won a Fields Medal. Now he trains his students to replicate the same method: the first one or two problems are assigned by him, and even he doesn't have the answers; he works alongside the student slowly through the third or fourth year, then lets them pose questions independently.

28:36 Spacetime isn't a background, it's an emergent approximation
Think of string theory the way you think of water being made of discrete atoms: the continuous spacetime we touch is very likely just a low-resolution approximation of some deeper structure at macroscopic scales. Gopakumar stresses this isn't pure speculation — quantum mechanics itself doesn't allow spacetime to be treated as an infinitely divisible smooth background; add black holes (Hawking and others found they have many anomalous properties) and the breakdown of the Big Bang at the singularity, and physicists have to answer ‘where does spacetime come from’. String theory happens to give a natural framework: spacetime emerges from something more fundamental, and gravity plus the known interactions can fit inside it. This explains why he treats ‘solving quantum gravity’ as a very high bar for intelligence: it demands not just problem-solving, but building a new conceptual framework.

39:45 Materials should be designed in reverse: set the property, then find the structure
Start with a long-cycle yardstick: quantum mechanics was originally just for understanding atoms, and the devices it now underpins account for roughly 35%-40% of US GDP by his estimate, while the commercial ripples only became obvious four or five decades after the theory appeared. He calls the current phase the second quantum revolution: ‘accidental discovery’ quantum materials like graphene are already commercializing, and the next step is inverse materials design with AI — first define what performance the material needs, then search for what structure can deliver it and how to synthesize it, bypassing traditional trial-and-error chemistry. He also reveals a conversation with Demis Hassabis: DeepMind's next holy grail is finding a room-temperature superconductor, and Hassabis told him from the start not to talk about quantum gravity.

50:59 Being stuck is the norm; keep three or four problems in play at once
Being stuck isn't the exception, it's a researcher's daily life; especially during the student-to-researcher transition, being stuck can feel like a crush (being overwhelmed). Gopakumar's first strategy is portfolio hedging: push three or four problems at once, and when one dies, switch to another — probabilistically at least one will move half a step. The second move is to go teach — the moment a student's eyes light up, that satisfaction can pull you out of a trough, and he has repeatedly found that ‘after a lecture, the stuck problem suddenly opens up’. The third move is to deliberately learn something new you've always wanted to learn but never had time for, to switch to a new frame of reference before returning to the old problem.

55:08 Talent is multiplicative, not additive; the shortage is never headcount
Why does top-tier science cluster in a few places rather than distribute evenly? Gopakumar gives the mechanism: talking in the same place, using each other as sounding boards — even without formal collaboration, the brain stays in a stimulated state; and once real collaboration happens, the different skills two people bring are multiplicative rather than additive. He borrows a physics metaphor: photons in an ordinary light bulb are chaotic, photons in a laser are coherent with each other, and once a group of people forms coherence they too produce a lasing effect. He says many Indian institutions actually underperform their talent, and what's missing isn't headcount but this resonant atmosphere; hence ICTS's founding principle is simple — hire only first-rate people, give them resources and freedom, and don't let them lower their ambitions.

1:11:19 AI can accelerate research, but it can't make conceptual leaps
AI just won two Nobel Prizes in a row, but Gopakumar splits ‘AI for science’ and ‘science for AI’ into two things: the former he grants is an overdrive gear, with AI accelerating a certain very narrow class of tasks in research; but the ‘theory’ AI does today is still far from his conceptual-layer standard, and the best physics relies on conceptual leaps rather than pattern recognition. Conversely, he's more bullish on science for AI — among the people who discovered scaling laws at Anthropic are physicists by training; Hopfield himself was a statistical physicist, using simple physical models to simulate the brain. Along this path, physicists might join computer scientists and neuroscientists to take AI from language models to physics-inspired world models. This distinction is worth remembering.

1:21:32 After the synthesizability gate, AI's new materials come to zero
The soberest bucket of cold water in the whole session came from the audience Q&A: Google claims to have discovered a large number of new materials with AI, but after filtering out feasibility and the synthesizability gate, Gopakumar's phrasing is ‘I think left with zero’ — zero left. His stance isn't to deny AI materials science (someone in the same session cited Microsoft's DFT model with only 385,000 parameters that bypasses traditional hybrid methods), but to remind that the whole chain is still long: after predicting a crystal structure you still have to grow it and scale it, and every step can filter out the surprises. He says India should also bet on this chain. This line is a useful reverse calibration for the ‘AI discovers new materials’ narrative.

item.title: AI's Frontrunners Are Just Refineries, Not the Native-App Winners
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-zhangxiaojun-ai没有安全巨头-公司制度将消亡/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-03-zhangxiaojun-ai没有安全巨头-公司制度将消亡/
item.description: AI has entered the agent stage: the first-stage frontrunners are just refineries, not the native-app winners; new platforms don't come from old platforms, organizations must shift from jobs to tasks, and in the end what people compete on is the creativity to conjure something from nothing.
item.content:encoded:
AI has entered the agent stage: the first-stage frontrunners are just refineries, not the native-app winners; new platforms don't come from old platforms, organizations must shift from jobs to tasks, and in the end what people compete on is the creativity to conjure something from nothing.

Zeng Ming gives you a coordinate system for judging where AI sits, using a three-stage industrial history. It's a cure for the optimism of "this time is different," and it offers application founders a window of opportunity along with a brutal forecast for incumbents' transformation.

16:28 Building agents today is like building websites in 1992
Zeng Ming divides the industrialization of a general-purpose technology into three stages: first it becomes social infrastructure, then applications explode, and finally native applications appear. In 2026, token as a unit of measurement reaching consensus shows the first stage has matured; the agent events around Chinese New Year (commonly called "lobster") mark AI's formal entry into the agent stage. He draws an analogy to the 1992 website-building movement: people then were building websites to share information, today they're building agents to share capabilities. The browser hasn't appeared yet, and whoever can establish agent standards and seize the user entry point may be the biggest opportunity of the next two years.

27:49 A ten-trillion-dollar company will appear, but not these two
Zeng Ming says plainly that OpenAI and Anthropic are remarkable technological and commercial achievements, but business history shows the first wave of breakout companies is most likely not the big winners of the native-application stage. Yahoo reached a $120 billion market cap five years after founding, AOL was valued at $220 billion, and neither became the Google of the next era. Model companies are more like AI cloud companies, refineries that refine crude oil — the real application value belongs to chemical plants and car companies, and cars were not built by oil companies. He believes a ten-trillion-dollar company will certainly appear, but it may not be the two current frontrunners. Model companies will evolve into a mature business of oligopoly plus heavy government regulation.

1:10:29 The unit of an AI-native organization is the task, not the job
The company corresponds to the industrial-age hierarchy; AI disrupts the industrial age, and the corporate system will wither. The basic unit of an AI-native organization is not the job but the task: people are not organized by reporting lines but flow around "what needs to be solved," and both humans and AI coordinate around tasks. So well-designed jobs and hierarchies will disappear, and the traditional middle layer will die out too; future founders must first define the organization's task network. Silicon Valley's NewLab is a prototype of the new organizational form, and OpenAI itself is more like a Lab than a traditional company. The culture of the new organization is more like a sports team, emphasizing transparency, sharing, and co-creation, no longer relying on commands and performance reviews.

1:31:32 Excellence is only determined afterward; being good is visible on the spot
Zeng Ming argues that "good ≠ excellent." Being good is growth that continuously receives positive feedback, while excellence requires overcoming negative feedback again and again, persisting when everyone disapproves, and ultimately proving through enormous success that you were the era's prophet — hence "excellence is determined afterward." Good people easily fall into a cycle of proving themselves, leading to conservative strategies. Excellent people have a small ego, tend to attribute success to the times and their partners, and are driven by mission rather than external valuation. When identifying founders, he asks, "Ten years from now, what kind of self would you be satisfied with?" If the answer is "a ten-billion-dollar company," that's mainly ego-driven, not an inner mission. Truly excellent founders are often altruistic and empathetic.

1:47:24 Strategy in the AI era cannot be planned, only generated
Strategy in the AI era is not planning but generation. Zeng Ming proposes a "strategy generation system": the organization must build an environment and network where strategic insight emerges naturally. Because decision frequency is higher and quality demands are greater, a CEO cannot plan by linear extrapolation, nor can strategy be outsourced to McKinsey — McKinsey's explosion was a product of the slow maturation of the industrial age. His methodology is "look ten years, think three years, do one year," with the core being "think three years": you must at least see two or three milestones, creating tension between short-term action and the mid-term picture. Organization building must ensure enough context rather than control, letting the right people make the right decisions at the right time.

2:01:39 The right analogy for robots is appliances, not cars
Zeng Ming believes robots are still in a period of strategic exploration, far from convergence. The current two paths — building a generalized brain first or closing the scenario loop first — are both logically valid, and it's impossible to judge in advance which is faster. By historical analogy, the auto industry had thousands of companies from 1900 to 1920, and only entered scale after Ford built the assembly line in 1913; robots haven't yet had their Model T moment, and whoever truly sells ten thousand robots first is already remarkable. But a better analogy for robots is appliances rather than cars: after electricity was invented, countless categories appeared — refrigerators, washing machines, air conditioners — and robots interacting in the physical world will have N kinds of big scenarios, with home, companionship, and industrial all potentially producing their own native giants.

2:03:39 The giants who feel safe are the least safe
Zeng Ming says that before a huge wave, no one is safe, and feeling safe is the most unsafe. In business history, no era's companies have smoothly transitioned to the next era; IBM and Microsoft are the only two possible exceptions, and both are full of uncertainty. AI is a productivity revolution that disrupts the industrial revolution, not a continuation-style innovation like mobile internet, so old giants' technological reserves and organizational culture are negative assets. Google can live on as an AI cloud company but may not capture the consumer entry point; ByteDance has an AI cloud opportunity, but Doubao is not the future application; Tencent's social relationships will be restructured; Alibaba is likewise not naturally safe. New platforms will most likely be created by new companies.

2:20:56 Human value lies in creating from nothing, not writing songs or painting
Drawing on Drucker's framework, Zeng Ming defines the AI era as the era of creativity: all knowledge work that can be structured will be taken over by AI, and people are both forced and finally liberated to develop new potential. That potential is creativity — not writing songs or painting, but the ability to originally define complex problems and conjure something from nothing. AI has already taken away all existing knowledge; human value lies in creating what does not yet exist. So he calls his mission "being a happy researcher," and believes civilization will next reorganize around creativity, even forcing the education system from "knowledge instillation" to "open exploration," because young people already know the old path leads nowhere.

item.title: AI writing's moat isn't the model, it's the proprietary data you feed it
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-aiandi-ai-写作的护城河不是模型-而是你喂进去的独家数据/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-aiandi-ai-写作的护城河不是模型-而是你喂进去的独家数据/
item.description: Over two years, Every writer Katie turned ChatGPT from a career coach during a layoff into a one-person content company and a compounding editor; the core method isn't prompts, it's using proprietary experience to cover the "last mile" the model can't reach.
item.content:encoded:
Over two years, Every writer Katie turned ChatGPT from a career coach during a layoff into a one-person content company and a compounding editor; the core method isn't prompts, it's using proprietary experience to cover the "last mile" the model can't reach.

Not a tool review, but how a non-technical writer uses AI as a mode of production: the substance is concentrated in the last 30 minutes, and the personal story up front provides the motivational context.

2:09 The AI coach's biggest value isn't saving money
After being laid off she was at a low point and couldn't afford a human career coach's hourly rate, but a $20-a-month ChatGPT subscription was acceptable. She found that writing her thoughts out and letting AI question and push back from the outside helped her externalize her thinking, fight catastrophizing, and gave her a sense of accountability. The most important legacy of that experience wasn't the money saved, but that it made her believe AI really can drive concrete change in a life. At the time she was wavering over whether to take Every's freelance offer, and it was ChatGPT that gave her the push to just try it.

8:26 Throughput comes from upfront context, not clever prompts
She once took on a delivery load of 8 blog posts, 3 ebooks, 24 LinkedIn posts, 24 X posts and 16 Instagram posts in a week and a half. She could do it not because she knew a smarter one-line prompt, but because she did a lot of upfront context engineering: feeding the model brand information, product details, audience profiles and differentiators all at once. Much of the demand was essentially content repurposing, and AI is good at rewriting one long piece into versions for different platforms. The rule she distilled: set the scene well up front, and only then can you run fast later.

11:28 Give the model a fence first, then talk tone and word choice
Before Claude Projects existed, she could only keep persistent documents in Google Docs and manually copy-paste them into context each time. This structure didn't fall from the sky; it comes from the style guide tradition in content marketing: first define who the audience is, what the pain points are, how the product maps to them, who the competitors are and where the differentiation lies. She says this amounts to giving the model a playground with a fence: first make sure it won't wander off, then talk word choice, tone and reading difficulty. Later, as soon as Projects launched, she built a separate project for every client and every column.

15:40 AI writing's last mile can only be covered by a human
She believes AI writing has a "last mile" problem: models have a knowledge cutoff, and they aren't in the real physical world. So the human's job is to supply the latest data and real experience that AI can't reach. She warns that if you just throw the model a single line like "write a blog post about style guides," all you'll get is the generic content it already knows, which is commoditized information; what actually makes writing unique is fresh ingredients the model has never seen, like internal company research, third-party reports and personal experience. The writing system is the kitchen; the human is responsible for providing good ingredients.

22:50 AI's value is reducing friction, not speeding up output
She talks openly about her bipolar disorder and points out that AI's value isn't just producing content faster, but reducing friction in life. She put off booking a primary care doctor for three years, and finally just had Codex find doctors who accept her insurance and are taking new patients and complete the booking; email is first filtered by automation, and only messages that genuinely need a human reply reach her inbox. She says this completely solved her email anxiety. This isn't treating AI as a production tool, but as assistive technology that makes her day-to-day running "as a person" easier.

27:03 Let AI interview you repeatedly, and it can prioritize for you
Two years ago she just asked ChatGPT whether it could be her career coach; today that coach lives in a Codex project containing her job profile, Every's brand positioning, content performance data, a reader-praise folder and OKRs. She doesn't maintain the board herself; she uses voice conversation to have the system prioritize by highest impact, and the system also maintains her Kanban for her. The key to building this system was having AI interview her repeatedly and then sedimenting those interviews into context. She says it's like having a Chief of Staff, not just a writer.

32:27 Feedback that only fixes the current draft is wasted
The core of the Compound Writing plugin is compounding thinking: every piece of feedback given to AI should flow back into the system so the next output is automatically better. She forked Kieran Klassen's Compound Engineering plugin and reworked it into a writing workflow: code and writing both have brainstorming, planning, drafting and review stages, except writing cares more about structure, voice and evidence. Editing is further split into a substantive edit that looks at big structure and argument, a line edit that works sentence by sentence, and a final pass that checks before publication. Now she doesn't write in a web chat window, but pours the day's fresh material into this system.

39:19 Vonnegut as editor gives you a perspective, not a verdict
She built Vonnegut's eight narrative elements, Hitchcock's suspense principle about the bomb under the table, and the expressive styles of Sorkin and Sedaris into the plugin as editing skills. Vonnegut checks whether "the story starts as close to the end as possible" and whether "every sentence earns its place"; Hitchcock's perspective asks whether the reader will want to keep reading because of this. She stresses that this isn't letting the masters' ghosts grade your draft, but giving you a new perspective you can accept or reject; non-professional writers may actually benefit more, because they're less likely to be picking at themselves while they write.

item.title: Stronger Models Make Dirty Data Deadlier: Cleaning It Is Worth More, Not Less
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-signalsandthre-模型越强-脏数据越致命-清洗反而更值钱/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-02-signalsandthre-模型越强-脏数据越致命-清洗反而更值钱/
item.description: Jane Street's alternative data team found that once data leaks future information into the past, the stronger the model, the more dangerous it gets; pinning down "what was known at the time" is worth more than tuning the model.
item.content:encoded:
Jane Street's alternative data team found that once data leaks future information into the past, the stronger the model, the more dangerous it gets; pinning down "what was known at the time" is worth more than tuning the model.

This episode is a dense account of how data engineering actually creates value, and the second half — on corrected data, timestamps and cost models — contains judgments you won't hear in most AI discussions.

2:06 Once a pattern is found, competition eats it
This is what Eric defines as an anti-inductive environment: in trading, the patterns you find are often quickly absorbed by other people and the market, and then stop working; knowledge that can accumulate over the long term like a law of physics is rare. Because of this, the signal-to-noise ratio of trading data is naturally ugly — the whole mechanism of the market is to keep squeezing out extractable signal, and what's left drifts ever closer to a random walk. To keep winning, you have to keep finding new facts, not sit on old patterns.

19:21 Prices can go negative — don't hard-code assumptions into the system
On April 20, 2020, the settlement price of near-expiry crude oil futures on the CME closed negative — just for that one day, and the final settlement price later returned to positive. The reason wasn't that oil had no value, but that storage space at the delivery point, Cushing, was nearly full and nobody wanted to take physical delivery. Order and risk systems that had long assumed prices must be positive failed on the spot: some people couldn't place orders, others didn't know how to handle negative returns. Eric's conclusion is that a large part of trading is understanding the boring details of reality: tank capacity, contract multipliers, quote units. Only when the system gets these details right can you draw a ceiling on risk.

32:33 Domain experts don't know how good good tools can be
For data and systems to be genuinely usable, the bottleneck is often not writing code but translation. Eric observes that traders have a high tolerance for painful workflows, worn down by Excel and manual processes to the point where they don't know they deserve better tools; conversely, software engineers who don't understand the trading domain can only build to a narrow spec. So his job is to explain the domain's real mechanics to engineers, and to explain "how good it could get" to traders. Jane Street now has such an embedded developer on every desk, and that role grew out of exactly this.

59:04 The number of parking spaces is not the sales figure
The classic example of alternative data is counting cars in Walmart parking lots — the more people in the cars, the better business is. Eric says this example is actually terrible: what you want to infer is consumer spending, but parking spaces only tell you foot traffic, very indirectly; about 20% of Walmart shopping happens online, and a city like New York has no parking lots to count. The more direct signal is on the transaction side: card-issuing banks, the Visa/Mastercard networks, and credit union processing systems know how much people actually spent, and can sell anonymised aggregate statistics to buyers.

1:04:08 Corrected data turns a backtest into a time machine
When deciding whether to subscribe to a dataset, the vendor may already have corrected past errors; backtesting on the pretty corrected data doesn't test the data you would actually have received back then, but the right answer you only learned later. Eric says this is equivalent to simulating that you own a time machine. Jane Street's solution is to keep every raw piece of data and the local timestamp at which it was received, so that no matter how many transformations you do later, you can reconstruct "what exactly we knew at that moment". This is the same logic as distrusting exchange timestamps and trusting only your own data's arrival time.

1:08:10 LLMs know the future — keep them away from historical data
AI hits alternative data on two levels: stronger predictive models raise the value of good data, and LLMs make it easy to extract features from text. But watch out for a causal trap — using the latest LLM to featurize old documents drags in what happened later: it knows how Enron ended, and it may have seen later revisions of that financial report in its training data. This amounts to creating a new future-information leak, and when handling historical data you especially need to pin down "which point-in-time model was used".

1:11:26 The stronger the model, the more data cleaning is worth
A common expectation is that as neural networks get stronger, feature engineering and manual cleaning will be replaced. Eric's view is the opposite: once models can do more on their own, you can do less manual feature work, but the data you feed in has to be more correct. If the data isn't point-in-time and quietly leaks future information into the past, stronger models will learn that problem; different models also have different tolerances for outliers and patches of dirty data. All told, cleaning data is worth more, not less.

1:16:34 Usage-based billing induces teams to keep saving money
Jane Street runs its data warehouse in its own data centre, and it isn't purely about control. Eric's observation is that moving the same queries to a cloud vendor billed by reads or compute time gets expensive enough that you feel "this money could buy a pile of hardware". More important is the distorting effect of the cost model — usage-based billing makes teams constantly optimise the bill and reshape workloads to accommodate the billing; once you build your own, cost becomes a one-off hardware investment, and the team spends its time on research and queries themselves rather than on saving money.

item.title: The Most Valuable Step in Writing With AI Isn't the Prompt — It's Compounding Your Edit Feedback
