item.description: The 1965 separation of Singapore and Malaysia was not Singapore being expelled by Malaysia — it was pushed through behind Lee Kuan Yew's back by his own negotiator, Goh Keng Swee. The archives uncover a founding narrative that was reconstructed after the fact.
item.content:encoded:
The 1965 separation of Singapore and Malaysia was not Singapore being expelled by Malaysia — it was pushed through behind Lee Kuan Yew's back by his own negotiator, Goh Keng Swee. The archives uncover a founding narrative that was reconstructed after the fact.

For listeners interested in Singapore's founding history and the Cold War landscape of Southeast Asia. Drawing on the newly declassified Albatross archives, the episode retraces the whole chain of events behind the separation and offers a perspective different from the official narrative.

4:03 The Albatross archives don't overturn history — they harden Goh Keng Swee's role as the separatist
It was only in 1994, while writing his memoirs, that Lee Kuan Yew was allowed to read the oral histories Goh Keng Swee recorded between 1980 and 1981, and learned for the first time that Goh had not, as instructed, pressed Tun Razak for a looser arrangement between the two sides. Lee wrote: "I knew they were single-mindedly determined that Singapore should withdraw from the federal parliament, so I had no choice but to follow their wishes and separate us out." The archives reinforce Goh Keng Swee's role as a more committed separatist than Lee Kuan Yew himself.

13:58 The "albatross" metaphor casts the Federation of Malaya as Singapore's burden
Goh Keng Swee invoked Coleridge's 1798 poem The Rime of the Ancient Mariner: the old sailor shoots the albatross for no reason, disaster breaks out on the ship, and the crew hangs the dead bird around his neck as an inescapable burden. Goh used it to refer to the Malaysian Federation — Singapore joined expecting a common market and full decolonisation, only to find itself continuously colonised by the new government in Kuala Lumpur: fewer parliamentary seats, higher taxes, with the tax burden on attap houses reaching 25%.

29:49 Operation Coldstore was the tribute Singapore paid for merger
On 2 February 1963, before the Federation of Malaysia was formally established, Britain, the government of the Federation of Malaya and the Singapore self-government formed a tripartite council and arrested 113 leftists in Singapore. This was seen as Singapore's show of sincerity to Kuala Lumpur — clearing out leftist forces as the price of admission to the Malaysian Federation. Lee Kuan Yew's non-communist faction thereby eliminated pro-communist rivals such as Lim Chin Siong, but the left-wing Barisan Sosialis still took with it more than half of the trade unions and local cadre networks.

35:49 Merger was built on institutional inequality
Kuala Lumpur feared the Chinese population would disrupt central politics, so of 159 parliamentary seats it gave Singapore only 12, suppressing its representation while demanding that Singapore bear higher taxes. This "no representation, high taxation" arrangement ran directly counter to Singapore's original aim of joining the federation in exchange for an economic hinterland. On citizenship policy, Singapore had always been permissive, while Malaya set multiple thresholds for Chinese and Indians seeking naturalisation — two sets of standards that formed a fundamental rift.

47:23 Lee Kuan Yew's ambition: replace the MCA and the MIC
A note in the Albatross archives titled "Post-Malaysia Situation" records Lee Kuan Yew's political roadmap: he had to guard against both the communist threat and Malay-supremacist racism. He judged that the People's Action Party would sooner or later replace the Malaysian Chinese Association and the Malaysian Indian Congress and become a partner UMNO would have no choice but to work with. He was confident that a "Malaysian Malaysia" campaign could force UMNO to concede under the pressures of Konfrontasi and Anglo-American pressure.

1:00:31 PAP leaders once planned a government-in-exile in Cambodia
The Albatross archives exhibition reveals that PAP leaders feared UMNO would wipe them out the way it had dealt with the left. Devan Nair and others had already conceived of a worst-case plan: using personal ties with Sihanouk to set up a government-in-exile in Cambodia and preserve the flame. This episode highlights the extreme risk assessment of Singapore's leaders at the time: they knew the playbook of arresting people could turn on them at any moment.

1:07:53 Goh Keng Swee tossed out the "separation" plan in casual conversation
A footnote in Lee Kuan Yew's notes records the day and the time — "half past five on which day" — when he realised Goh Keng Swee had deceived him. Goh never told Lee directly that UMNO might not insist on separation; the break-up was something he and Tun Razak proposed on their own initiative in the negotiations. Once the idea was spoken aloud, the wheels could not be stopped. Goh is described as a more committed separatist than Lee Kuan Yew — he pushed the separation plan through almost on his own authority, acting first and reporting afterwards.

1:22:24 The archives exhibition serves Singapore's "premeditated independence" national narrative
With refined lighting and 3D-to-4D interactive displays, the Albatross archives exhibition reshapes Singapore from "forced into independence" into "a destiny foreseen" — actively taking charge of its own fate. Goh Keng Swee called the separation the best gift to Singapore, and said the twelve months of negotiation defined what it means to be Singaporean. This narrative reinforcement looks increasingly important today, as it responds to global upheaval, new immigration and tariff wars.

item.title: Xiaomi's Three-Chip Blitz: Trading Resources for Time, Betting on an Edge-AI Paradigm Shift
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-01-laoshi-小米三芯齐发-激进造芯赌的是垂直整合与时间窗口/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-01-laoshi-小米三芯齐发-激进造芯赌的是垂直整合与时间窗口/
item.description: Xiaomi released three Xuanjie chips in one go, aggressively betting on memory interconnect, 3D stacking and an all-AI architecture — trading resources for time, wagering on an edge-AI paradigm shift and vertical integration capability, though a clear gap remains to the top chip companies.
item.content:encoded:
Xiaomi released three Xuanjie chips in one go, aggressively betting on memory interconnect, 3D stacking and an all-AI architecture — trading resources for time, wagering on an edge-AI paradigm shift and vertical integration capability, though a clear gap remains to the top chip companies.

This deep-dive parses the technical choices and strategic logic behind Xiaomi's three chips with high information density, especially offering clear metaphors for key technologies like memory interconnect and 3D stacking. Worth a listen for chip industry professionals and investors watching Xiaomi.

3:02 Whether a company can make chips depends on system definition power, not IP self-development rate
Judging whether a company can make chips isn't just about how many IPs it hand-built, but how much system definition power it holds. Although Xiaomi's Xuanjie O1 uses ARM IP for CPU and GPU, system integration and physical implementation are its own. Apple and Qualcomm are strong because they can iterate every year and keep taping out — exactly what latecomers lack most. Xiaomi doesn't have ten years to learn slowly, so it chose an aggressive route, pushing multiple high-risk technology lines simultaneously.

6:04 The culprit behind O1's unideal efficiency is the lack of a shared water tank
Xuanjie O1 lacks a system-level cache (SLC), so GPU power draw can't be contained under high load, and efficiency is unideal. SLC is like a shared water tank for a neighborhood: the closer data is to compute units, the faster the access and the lower the power. O1's GPU has many cores but limited DDR bandwidth, so many cores wait for data and utilization stays low — this is the bandwidth wall. O3 adds a 16MB SLC, split into multiple cache blocks distributed across the chip, and designs an on-chip network scheduling system to solve data consistency and access conflicts.

10:07 ARM's public bus is too generic, so Xuanjie had to build its own
ARM's public CHI+CMN solution is too generic, requiring compatibility and redundancy designs that are hard to customize for Xuanjie. O3 simply developed its own X-Ring unified fusion bus, compatible with CHI but defining its own interconnect protocol, with a self-developed high-speed road network scheduling center and memory controller. This means fewer protocol conversions, and data can decide cache location and path based on demand. Xiaomi data claims protocol conversion overhead reduced by 75%, static access latency of 82 nanoseconds, 32% lower than O1, even lower than Apple A19 Pro.

12:09 The compute bottleneck is shifting from matrix multiplication to vector operations
O3 adds an AI unit to every subsystem — CPU, GPU, ISP — letting computation happen where the data is, reducing data movement. NPU core count drops from 6 to 4, but Tensor compute rises to 200Tops, because Xiaomi judges that the large-model bottleneck is expanding from matrix multiplication to vector operations such as Softmax, quantization, KVCache, etc. The vector unit area is about the same as Tensor, with 6.8 times the number of multiply-accumulate units as O1, and introduces an SMT-like architecture, similar to CUDA, to handle irregular parallel tasks.

15:11 Chips and models should be defined together by the same company
Xiaomi partnered with MEMO, using a 5-value quantization method to compress INT4 weights to 5 bits with almost no precision loss, reducing memory bandwidth and capacity demand by 30%. The 3-billion-parameter MEMO model deployed on O3 improves prefill performance by 40% and decode by 45%. This ability to jointly define chips and models is the closed-loop advantage of vertical integration — no need to wait for others to define a model and then adapt.

16:11 3nm performance is squeezed out bit by bit from standard cells
O3 uses the more mature N3P process, improving performance by 5% at the same power, and reducing power by 5%-10% at the same frequency. Xiaomi also did extensive process optimization: self-developed standard cells increased from 480 in O1 to over 2,400, covering all chip units; compressing the power supply buffer channel so power and signals run through the middle of the module, increasing transistor density by 5%. CPU changed from 4 clusters to 3 clusters of 10 all-big cores, with single-core performance up 31%, multi-core up 60%, surpassing A19 Pro.

19:13 Near-memory computing pushes phone memory bandwidth to 1.22TB/s
Xuanjie O100 uses wafer-level 3D stacking, with one compute wafer and two memory wafers stacked vertically, interconnected via Hybrid Bonding, forming a near-memory computing architecture. It uses thousands of shorter, denser vertical connections to achieve high bandwidth, with lower energy per bit shifted, similar to HBM on mobile. Data: 28,762 data connections, bandwidth 1.22TB/s, far exceeding the tens-of-bits-wide connections of traditional SoC and LPDDR. The compute layer has 14 independent cores, each with a RISC-V processor for control.

21:17 ChangXin's value isn't in speed grades, but in joint definition
Xiaomi partnered with ChangXin to debut LPDDR6, reducing dependence on Samsung and SK Hynix. Even if ChangXin offers a starting grade of 10.667Gbps, Xiaomi can compensate for peak speed gaps through wider channels, larger SLC, and self-developed memory controllers. More importantly, the two sides jointly verify and tune from the design stage, jointly defining China's mobile memory subsystem solution. For ChangXin, it proves its high-speed IO and physical layer capabilities, earning a seat at the new-generation mobile memory table.

item.title: The Agent Bottleneck Isn't Context, It's Memory: Write, Change, Recall, Forget
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-01-cogrev-agent-的瓶颈不在上下文-在记忆的写改召回遗忘/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-01-cogrev-agent-的瓶颈不在上下文-在记忆的写改召回遗忘/
item.description: Uber burning through its token budget in 13 weeks proves stuffing context is wrong; MongoDB points the Agent performance bottleneck at memory — write, change, recall, forget — and suggests starting with employee use cases and human-in-the-loop.
item.content:encoded:
Uber burning through its token budget in 13 weeks proves stuffing context is wrong; MongoDB points the Agent performance bottleneck at memory — write, change, recall, forget — and suggests starting with employee use cases and human-in-the-loop.

This episode clears obstacles for people doing Agent engineering: how to set chunk size, the 100k vector threshold, who writes and deletes memory; of little value to those who only want to hear about model progress.

6:32 Database schemas follow whatever resource is scarcest
Pete takes E.F. Codd's 1970 relational model paper as a starting point: storage was the most expensive thing then, so normalized tables were the rational choice. When MongoDB was born in 2007, the scarce resource had become time, so the document model deliberately denormalizes, using JSON/BSON to reduce disk reads. He also corrects a repeatedly misread positioning: MongoDB is not ‘schemaless’ but ‘schema-flexible’ — the same collection can hold documents of different shapes, letting schema evolve along with the product. This design logic shows: a database schema should follow whatever resource is scarcest at the time.

16:38 Stuffing data into context actually lowers quality
The news that Uber burned through its 2026 token budget in 13 weeks is treated as a sample of token maxing strategy failing. Stuffing large amounts of data into context is only half a cost problem; quality also drops: research shows the first and last few thousand tokens of a window matter most, while the middle is basically noise. This path pushes the industry toward ‘categorical memory’ — each turn selects only the few terms relevant to the current agent loop, rather than dumping all history back in. The key here is not saving money, but that attention decay inside the context makes selective retrieval a performance problem.

23:21 AI features should grow from where customers already hurt
MongoDB's search capabilities grew layer by layer from customer pain points: in 2020 it first did lexical search, because many customers were building their own Lucene; then vector search, because a vector is essentially a float array and can naturally be a document field; then it built lexical, vector and metadata pre-filtering into the same hybrid search. In 2025 it simply acquired Voyage AI, bringing the embedding model in too, forming a ‘better together’ solution. This order itself shows: when infrastructure companies touch AI features, they usually start from where customers already hurt, rather than buying a model first and then creating a scenario.

40:10 Chunk size should be left to the model, not human trial and error
The first grinding problem in RAG is chunk size: too small, not enough context, poor retrieval quality; too large, storage grows and precision actually drops, leaving only manual repeated testing. Voyage's ‘contextual chunking’ sends the sentence and extra context as two separate strings into the model, letting the model automatically determine the optimal chunk size, and finally returns only one vector. This way you can use very small chunks to get retrieval quality close to full context, with lower storage cost, and it is now at version four. This is a concrete example of moving the engineer's repeated parameter tuning into the model weights.

48:20 Embedding models haven't been commoditized; model choice determines hallucination
Pete gives two selection thresholds: on scale, vector volume only really starts to hurt around 100k; on quality, Voyage leads on the Hugging Face RTEB benchmark, improving up to 14% over other embedding models, and this gap may directly show up as whether there is hallucination. He also reminds that embedding models have not been commoditized — Anthropic doesn't build an embedding model itself, so his advice is to just use Voyage. For many teams, embedding model selection has long been underestimated; this segment puts it back at the center of performance and hallucination.

1:01:05 Memory has a half-life and must be actively retired
Why is memory hard? Pete's analogy: the industry has been building databases for sixty years, but doing agents for only about eighteen months. The long-term context strategy is no longer stuffing the whole session back in, but recalling the best context at query time, and writing new facts back to memory after answering; enterprise systems also use RBAC to control memory sharing and isolation. He sums up the whole cycle with a colleague's words: Write, change, recall, forget. Memory has a half-life; recent information matters more than information from weeks or even months ago. This means agent memory must be treated as a first-class citizen, with intentional writing, updating and retiring.

1:13:10 The first wave of enterprise AI lands on employees, not customers
Most Fortune 500 companies Pete encounters are doing employee-facing use cases, and keeping humans in the loop. There are two layers to the reason: ROI is easier to calculate, these roles already have KPIs; the data security consequences are lighter, employee data leaks are easier to handle than customer data leaks. Conversely, fully autonomous customer-facing Agents are a bet with a worse risk-reward ratio right now. This segment provides a coordinate for enterprise AI budget judgment: the first wave of adoption is more likely to happen in internal efficiency tools, not robots making final decisions for customers.

1:24:24 The most complex customers aren't in the US, they're in Mexico City and São Paulo
Pete met this year's most complex customers in Mexico City and São Paulo, and these customers usually assume US competitors are more advanced. He says what he saw was exactly the opposite. The reason is attributed to the spread of hyperscale data centers and AI services; geographic barriers matter less than in the cloud era, and the ability of global enterprises to access technology has been leveled. This observation shows that judging whether a company can use frontier AI, the country label is increasingly unreliable.

item.title: The Fed Chair Never Loses a Vote: Warsh Talks Against Guidance, but He's Already Paving the Way for Hikes
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-01-oddlots-warsh演讲只是b-嘴上反指引-身体要加息/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-01-oddlots-warsh演讲只是b-嘴上反指引-身体要加息/
item.description: Posen gives Warsh's Jackson Hole speech a B-, arguing that he talks against forward guidance while actually paving the way for hikes, and predicts the Fed will raise rates 75-100 basis points over the next six months.
item.content:encoded:
Posen gives Warsh's Jackson Hole speech a B-, arguing that he talks against forward guidance while actually paving the way for hikes, and predicts the Fed will raise rates 75-100 basis points over the next six months.

Posen is one of the few central-bank watchers willing to say ‘fiscal dominance’ out loud; this episode delivers hard judgments on Fed governance risk, Powell's record, and AI's employment impact, at high information density.

4:07 Warsh never said he'd hike, but the whole speech paved the way
Posen gives Warsh's Jackson Hole speech a B-, though he says it could be treated as a B+ given the chaos of the preceding two months. The fourth section of the speech systematically lists reasons inflation could persist or even rise, yet never says ‘therefore we must tighten.’ Posen reads this as deliberate groundwork: if there are no hikes next, the market will suspect this is capitulation to pressure from Trump. Posen himself has argued for hikes for months, because inflation is real. Warsh also made clear the 2% core PCE target and refused to use wage inflation as a forecasting indicator — all mainstream moves.

8:14 Without defining the ‘right speed,’ returning to target is an empty phrase
What worries Posen most is that Warsh said at the end of the speech that inflation needs to fall in the ‘right direction’ at the ‘right speed,’ without ever defining what the right speed is. Without a speed constraint, ‘returning to target’ is an empty phrase. From his confirmation hearing to two press conferences to the ECB Sintra speech, Warsh has consistently reserved the right to ‘decide at the last minute,’ refusing to pre-commit to his own observation indicators. This is close to Greenspan's style in 1999, but Greenspan held up through personal ability and control of the committee; once he erred, the entire credibility would collapse with it.

12:20 The Fed chair never loses a vote
Posen explains the culture of the Fed committee: unlike the ECB, which seeks consensus, the Fed has historically given the chair more power. More critically, there is an unwritten rule — each meeting has only a few dissents, and the chair never loses a vote. When Volcker found he might lose a vote, he simply announced it would be his last meeting. This culture leaves the committee weak at correcting the chair, so Warsh's ‘reserve discretion’ style carries more risk than he imagines.

19:26 Criticizing the central bank isn't dangerous; making it help sell Treasuries is
Posen distinguishes two kinds of political pressure: ordinary criticism of the central bank is part of the game, and can even help the central bank ‘take the blame’ when necessary. What is truly dangerous is when a president or treasury secretary asks the central bank to help sell Treasuries; the central bank must then answer: ‘I am here to help you and your successor sell Treasuries,’ and must never manipulate or cheat. Trump's threats to the Fed are far more serious than rhetoric — trying to strip regional Fed presidents of voting rights, scrambling staggered terms, changing the mandate, touching the budget — these directly destroy functional independence.

24:34 The most radical reform may be making the central bank talk less
Posen thinks the communications committee led by Mervyn King is most likely to produce a radical proposal. King himself is a founder of inflation targeting and fan charts, but since retiring he has publicly doubted the central bank's forecasting ability and information supply: too much noise makes markets depend on official guidance, creating moral hazard and bubbles. Peter Fisher agrees, arguing that central bank ‘certainty’ makes markets less risk-sensitive. The two could push for less information disclosure rather than more. The ‘hall of mirrors’ metaphor in Warsh's speech already concedes that markets are not necessarily right.

34:51 Economists who join AI companies lose their independent voice
Posen argues that economists flocking to AI companies is not unprecedented — it happened during the internet era too — but this time it is more troubling. Companies like Anthropic hire economists partly to design AI transition policy, and these scholars genuinely believe they are doing good. The problem is that once inside, they enter the corporate hierarchy, lose their independent voice and freedom to choose topics, and their views get reasonably discounted by outsiders. Posen's hope is that scholars stay in research institutes, take low-six-figure salaries, and still have public influence.

38:53 AI replacement hasn't happened yet; programmer employment is still growing
Posen says labor market data does not yet show AI replacement — even employment growth for programmers and truck drivers continues. Brynjolfsson's J-curve theory holds that firms need time to reorganize their businesses, and humans and AI will first have a period of collaboration. Garicano's messy jobs theory points out that the jobs most easily automated actually contain a lot of tacit knowledge and human relationships — a truck driver, for example, does more than drive. Large-scale replacement may take about five years, and will show up first as reduced hiring of young people.

54:13 In six months rates will be 75-100 basis points higher than now
Posen reiterates his earlier forecast that year-end PCE inflation will hit 4%, which is now materializing; CPI already exceeded 4% early in the year. The bigger problem is inflation inertia: although energy prices may pull the numbers down slightly over the next month or two, core services inflation is stubborn, and the 3/6/12-month moving averages are all rising. He expects the Fed to hike in September or December; if it hikes in September it will hike again in December, and in six months the federal funds rate will be 75-100 basis points higher than now, only then will inflation truly start to fall, spending the interim in a 3.5%-4.5% range.

item.title: ECT Is Not Torture: 70% Respond, 60% Remit
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-01-tpwky-ect-不是酷刑-是精神科最有效的疗法之一/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-01-tpwky-ect-不是酷刑-是精神科最有效的疗法之一/
item.description: ECT brings about response in roughly 70% of patients and makes symptoms disappear in 60%; it is not the electrocution of One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, but the oldest somatic treatment to survive from the slaughterhouse to the anti-psychiatry movement.
item.content:encoded:
ECT brings about response in roughly 70% of patients and makes symptoms disappear in 60%; it is not the electrocution of One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, but the oldest somatic treatment to survive from the slaughterhouse to the anti-psychiatry movement.

Historical narratives usually fall into two extremes: either barbaric torture or miracle cure. This episode puts efficacy, abuse, media amplification and patient testimony side by side, so you can see where the stigma comes from and why it is not the whole picture today.

1:03 The heaviest side effect is not memory loss, it is stigma
The opening is told by Elan, a nurse, about her own experience: she was depressed from childhood, and after medication failed she chose ECT. She says that after three treatments, colors seemed turned up in saturation and the world became approachable again. The side effects are real: for days after treatment she could not find nouns, got lost in familiar neighborhoods, and lost words mid-conversation; remote memories from before treatment were still there, but felt like a room that had been rearranged. She states plainly that the heaviest side effect is the stigma surrounding ECT — she worried that sharing her experience would change how others saw her, and she believes that stigma is exactly why doctors did not recommend ECT earlier.

7:53 Fear of ECT is not innate, it was taught by film and television
A global survey of film and television published in 2016 found that 81% of movies and 72% of TV shows portrayed ECT inaccurately and negatively. In the most famous example, One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, Jack Nicholson is strapped down and shocked while conscious, a scene that is close to torture. A few positive portrayals exist, such as Homeland and Call the Midwife, but they are rare. The hosts' judgment is that public fear of ECT did not arise from nothing; it is a media stigma reinforced over decades, and it makes people unwilling even to consider ECT.

13:07 ECT is the most effective psychiatric intervention available
ECT treats severe mental illness such as treatment-resistant depression by passing electric current through the brain to induce a seizure; today it must be given under anesthesia and muscle relaxation, with strict informed consent. Two figures are often overlooked: about 70% of people respond and about 60% achieve clinical remission, making it one of the most effective psychiatric interventions available. Compared with the patient feedback the show saw when it previously covered SSRIs, it is especially effective in treatment-resistant cases where antidepressants alone have failed.

17:09 Electricity is only the tool; the target was always the seizure
The shock therapies that appeared in the 1920s were initially unrelated to electricity: insulin coma therapy put patients into hypoglycemic coma and convulsions, and Metrosol chemical shock therapy used drugs to induce seizures. Doctors persisted down this road because it was observed at the time that epilepsy and schizophrenia seemed rarely to coexist, and some catatonic patients improved after spontaneous seizures, so the seizure itself was taken to be the key therapeutic ingredient. Cerletti later wanted a safer, more tolerable way to induce seizures, which is why he turned to electricity. Electricity is only the tool; the target is the seizure.

22:14 ECT's technical starting point was pigs in a slaughterhouse
Cerletti's starting point was the slaughterhouse: workers would shock pigs to stun them, and some pigs had seizures after the shock. In April 1938, a man on the streets of Rome who spoke incoherently and had been brought to the hospital by police became the first human subject. There was no anesthesia and no muscle relaxant, and the first two shocks failed to induce a seizure. After the third, higher dose produced a grand mal seizure, the patient briefly stopped breathing and turned cyanotic, and only after forty-five seconds did he take a long breath and return to normal. Cerletti later reported 36 cases: 11 complete remissions, 20 improvements, 5 unchanged.

31:26 It spread so fast because there was no informed consent
By 1941, only three years after the first human trial, 42% of psychiatric hospitals in the United States had ECT machines. Several reasons explain the rapid spread: it was seen as an improved version of existing shock therapies and had a low barrier to entry; doctors had run out of options for chronic, severely ill patients; ECT was not the only therapy but often formed a recovery path alongside psychotherapy; early patient reports were generally positive; and at the time there was no informed consent and no patient protections requiring longer trial periods. That last point is precisely what planted the seeds of later widespread distrust of psychiatry.

36:34 Using ECT as punishment was not a film invention
The negative history is not a film invention: some institutions used ECT to treat homosexuality or hysteria; a 1940s account admitted that the amnesia and disorientation caused by shock could quiet patients and keep them from disrupting the ward. Such abuse occurred mostly in institutions with fewer resources and more marginalized patients, not in every hospital, but when exposed it provoked enormous public outrage. The anti-psychiatry movement then went on to call mental illness itself a form of social control. The hosts do not excuse these acts; they only remind us that at the time there were no effective drugs, wards were severely overcrowded, and doctors and families alike were trapped in despair.

42:45 The anti-psychiatry movement actually forced out ECT's evidence
The anti-psychiatry movement caused ECT use to fall sharply in the 1960s and 1970s, but it also forced ECT to undergo stricter scrutiny and randomized controlled trials. The result is that it is the only major somatic treatment that has withstood testing and survived from before psychopharmacology. After the 1980s, public accounts by Dick Cavett, Carrie Fisher and psychologist Norman Endler brought positive narratives back. Memory loss remains a real controversy: studies say long-term effects are rare, but some patients believe their experience is not adequately captured by the measurement tools. The experience cannot be reduced to one star or five stars; it should be neither mythologized nor stigmatized.

item.title: A State Court Authorized the Security Test, but the Sheriff Said the Contract Was Void
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-01-darknetdiaries-持州法院授权测安防-警长却说合同无效/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-01-darknetdiaries-持州法院授权测安防-警长却说合同无效/
item.description: A state court's authorization letter has no power over a county courthouse building, so a commissioned security test becomes burglary. Even after all charges are dropped, the arrest record stays on the books forever — the justice system can pay money, but it cannot restore a clean record.
item.content:encoded:
A state court's authorization letter has no power over a county courthouse building, so a commissioned security test becomes burglary. Even after all charges are dropped, the arrest record stays on the books forever — the justice system can pay money, but it cannot restore a clean record.

It explains the fragility of an "authorization contract" more clearly than any exploit: the owner of a building can overturn the entire paper trail, and legal accountability is almost entirely blocked by immunity. Anyone in security outsourcing or on the vendor side of a project should pause here.

12:07 A verbal agreement is no authorization at all
The rules document was only 28 pages, which makes it easy to assume the written contract had locked everything down. But Gary says the truly detailed agreements were almost all made verbally over the phone; if everything had been written down, the contract would have been a hundred pages long and no one would have signed it. That compromise planted the mine directly: when they later tested the Dallas County Courthouse, the verbally agreed scope did not cover that building — so procedurally they walked into a building that had "no authorization." The sheriff's later claim of "no authorization" had its roots not in technology but in a contract that was insufficient to cover every verbal conversation.

35:18 The building's owner outranks the authorization letter
Before the sheriff arrived they were still confident, because the contract stated in black and white that the state court had authorized it. But the sheriff's only response was: they don't own this courthouse, and I don't care whether you have a contract. Only then did Gary and Justin understand that a building's right of use and its contractual rights are separate; no matter how formal the contract signed by the state court, it could not make a door decision on behalf of the county court that owned the building. The mood on the spot turned from relaxed to arrest, and they had not even been worried before, because no tester in the industry had ever been prosecuted. This time was different.

48:28 The judge heard the truth as a lie
The judge told Gary, "You must think I'm stupid" — her reasoning being: if the state government had authorized this test, she, as a state employee, should have known; she didn't know, so it could only be a lie. Gary later said this judge had faced criminals' lies for so long that she could no longer tell what the truth was. A reasonable but dangerous logic: in a courtroom full of lies, an alibi-style contract actually looks more fake. Professional reports and legal process all failed in this scenario.

1:03:39 Dropping the charges does not erase the record
On January 30, 2020, all charges were dropped, but both men's criminal records will forever say they were arrested on burglary charges. Justin says they were deprived of their rights without due process — in many American background checks, an arrest record is just as conspicuous as a conviction. A dismissal only means no prosecution; it cannot erase the collateral consequences of that arrest: job hunting, passing through customs, going through security screening, this passage will follow them. The clean record they won through their criminal fight was really only half won.

1:17:45 The government refuses to answer for its mistakes through immunity
Holding anyone accountable was far harder than they imagined. They wanted to sue the sheriff, the prosecutor and the judge, but the system put up two walls: qualified immunity protects individuals acting in their official duties, and sovereign immunity says you cannot sue the government without its consent. The state court dismissed first — because the state government was the defendant; the federal court kicked the case back to the state, and the state dismissed it again. This was not a judge deciding a case, but a system in which no entry point exists for "the government was wrong." The only thing victims can sue is the office, not the person sitting in it; the sheriff personally does not have to pay a single cent. Judicial checks and balances here became an idle adjective.

1:31:56 You have to win the judicial lottery to get back a little dignity
Almost every wrongful arrest case dies in the same place: over 95% are dismissed because of qualified immunity, and most of the rest end in zero damages or a government victory. To get more than fifty thousand dollars in compensation, the odds are like winning the lottery, unless you were wrongly locked up for weeks or even months. Gary and Justin were held only one night, yet their evidence was airtight, and they ultimately got a rare public statement at the arbitration: it was not a question of whether they would win, but of how much money they could get. Near trial, the county offered a settlement of three hundred thousand dollars each, six hundred thousand total. But for them, that money could not buy back the half-life already written into the record.

item.description: ResNet is the most cited paper of the 21st century, but its real contribution is not making networks deeper — it invented the residual stream, a kind of working memory that lets a model store and edit information, and that changed how we understand neural networks.
item.content:encoded:
ResNet is the most cited paper of the 21st century, but its real contribution is not making networks deeper — it invented the residual stream, a kind of working memory that lets a model store and edit information, and that changed how we understand neural networks.

This episode uses clear animations and experiments to explain why residual connections work, how they gave rise to the Transformer, and the evidence that the residual stream acts as working memory. Suited to anyone who wants to understand the essence of modern AI architecture.

2:07 Deeper networks perform worse, not better
In early 2015, Sun Jian's team used careful initialization to push a network to 30 layers, but performance got worse than 14 layers (error rate 16.59% vs 13.34%). In theory, a 30-layer model could match a 14-layer one at minimum via identity mappings, but the optimizer cannot find such a solution. This suggests the problem is not network capacity but the training process itself.

15:18 Shattered gradients are the root disease of deep networks
By visualizing the loss landscape, they found that as depth increases, the loss surface of early layers becomes extremely rugged and gradient directions turn as random as white noise — the ‘shattered gradients problem’. Gradients are the core learning signal; once they fail, deep networks cannot be trained effectively.

17:18 Residual connections: an almost absurdly simple fix
Sun Jian's team's solution was laughably simple: between every two layers, add the input tensor directly to the output, forming a skip connection. This gives activations and gradients a direct path and effectively eliminates the shattered gradients problem. A 74-layer network with skip connections jumped from 38.9% to 72.6% accuracy, sweeping the major 2015 vision competitions.

20:19 ResNet overturned hierarchical representation theory
A Cornell team found that deleting or even shuffling ResNet's layers has little effect on performance. This contradicted the then-mainstream hierarchical representation theory — the idea that each layer builds on the previous one, so deleting any layer should be catastrophic. It forced the field to rethink: ResNet may not be learning hierarchical features but iteratively refining a ‘residual stream’ that runs through the whole network.

26:26 The residual stream: modern AI's hidden backbone
Straighten out the skip connections and you see an unbroken stream of data from input to output, with each layer only making incremental edits on top. This ‘residual stream’ later became a core design of the Transformer and a cornerstone of modern AI. Note, though, that follow-up work shows ResNet both learns hierarchical representations and refines the residual stream — the two can coexist.

29:28 The residual stream is the model's working memory
A Meta team found that in a vision Transformer's residual stream, activations at certain positions are unusually large and concentrated in unimportant regions of the image. They hypothesized the model treats these positions as ‘registers’ for aggregating global information. Experiments confirmed it: embeddings from these high-activation positions perform astonishingly well on image classification (85.2% vs 10.8%), and after adding extra ‘register tokens’, the model no longer occupies image positions.

item.title: The Fed's Credibility Cracks, and the Options Market Shrugs
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-excessreturns-美联储信誉崩塌-期权市场却当无事发生/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-excessreturns-美联储信誉崩塌-期权市场却当无事发生/
item.description: The Fed's credibility broke on a single decision not to hike, while the options market still prices Fed day like any other day — the cheapest insurance may be an illusion.
item.content:encoded:
The Fed's credibility broke on a single decision not to hike, while the options market still prices Fed day like any other day — the cheapest insurance may be an illusion.

Three pieces of evidence — sticky inflation, the midterms, and Fed credibility — point at the same thing: volatility is too low and cheap protection is a mirage. The frameworks and the data are both concrete.

3:03 A Fed without forward guidance is flipping a coin
The two hosts open with what has changed: at past FOMC meetings the market knew the odds with near certainty in advance, whereas this time the probability of a hike at the next meeting is only 55 to 45 — barely better than a coin flip. Add Warsh's Jackson Hole statement that he wants to fade forward guidance, and every meeting from here can turn into ‘see the result first, then react.’ Rate surprises transmit through debt and leverage into every asset, so volatility has to be repriced. The hosts also assert, based on history, that once the market truly tests them, almost every official eventually folds — so this current commitment to ‘never give the market expectations in advance’ is itself the most testable variable.

17:31 Midterm volatility is priced like an ordinary day
Kevin Muir thinks midterm volatility is badly underpriced. During the 2022 midterms, the options market priced a single-day S&P move of ±1.8% for voting day; in 2018 it was ±1.25%; now it is only ±0.9%. And this time Trump's approval is at historic lows, and he has just used a primetime address to talk about ‘election fraud’ for an hour, as if paving the way to challenge the result. Muir is careful to say: it's fine if you think he's overthinking it — as voting day approaches, the question of whether the election will be disrupted will itself get repriced. With volatility near seasonal lows and implied correlation also at historic lows, the odds on being long volatility are far better than usual.

23:41 The inflation pullback is a supply illusion; demand hasn't cooled
Ahan Manon breaks the PCE components into ‘demand-driven’ and ‘supply-driven.’ Right now the contributions are 3.31 versus 0.38; even if you strip out the energy supply shock from the Iran situation entirely, the remaining demand side alone is enough to keep inflation above the Fed's 2% target. Historically, demand-driven inflation is slow and persistent, while supply-driven inflation tends to spike fast and mean-revert within 6 to 12 months. The breadth is the bigger problem: in recent months, 70% to 80% of PCE components rose more than 2%. June briefly went negative month-over-month and July only rebounded 16 basis points, but that short-term cooling came almost entirely from the supply side; the demand-driven trend has not been interrupted.

34:51 One hike could have fixed the credibility; he didn't do it
Ben Hunt says Warsh shot himself in the foot at the press conference after the July meeting. The new face's debut and tough inflation talk had repaired the ‘Fed credibility’ narrative substantially; but what was actually needed was an immediate 25 basis point hike. Do it just once and the market believes ‘he means what he says,’ and no repeated hiking is needed afterward. Skip that step and the narrative flips completely: every independent piece that appeared in the financial media that week was saying the same thing in different words — ‘meet the new boss, same as the old boss.’ Once credibility shatters it is hard to glue back; the August gold rally was precisely the market's reaction to ‘hawkish talk, no action.’

40:13 After credibility is damaged, only verbal financial repression is left
Ben Hunt lists four pressures the Fed and Treasury must handle but absolutely cannot let blow up: the Iran war has no easy exit and oil stays higher for longer; fiscal stimulus effects are fading and tariff pressure is coming back; the insurance sector has a systemic problem of captive insurers being used to warehouse private investments; and 10-year and 30-year long-end yields above all cannot be pushed higher by the market. Any one of these could be the fuse for the next financial crisis. Handling them requires credibility, and credibility has just been damaged, so every policy option left is ‘verbal financial repression’ — using statements and intervention to hold yields down rather than letting the market price them. His judgment: this operation has no maturity date, it only accelerates.

49:25 The options market treats the Fed meeting as an ordinary day
The options term structure Brent Kachuba shows has almost no event risk: the S&P 0DTE straddle on the day of Warsh's speech was worth only 38 index points; SPX options expiring August 31 carried implied volatility of just 7%; the overall term structure sits at a 90-day low, and put open interest is very low. He normally avoids trading Fed events, because an event turns options into a kind of ‘tax’ — you collect premium before the event, and time value decays the moment it passes. What's special this time is that the market has crushed expected volatility to near zero and nobody is buying protection; before Jackson Hole he bought a few ‘lottery tickets’ with extremely cheap short-dated put spreads, because if Warsh says one thing the market doesn't want to hear, naked option sellers get flattened instantly. Once the event passes is the better time to chase directional trends.

58:42 Outsource the writing and you outsource the thinking
The closing topic is the Druckenmiller column handed to the WSJ: he said publicly it was written with AI, for the simple reason that AI writes better than he does. The two hosts argue the core question is whether the views and the emotion belong to the author; Druckenmiller's piece reads like his usual intuitive judgment, with AI only organizing and expressing it, so it isn't deception. Ben Hunt draws the line at the writing itself: writing is part of the thinking process — ‘I write it down to figure out what I think.’ When the text-generation step is outsourced, readers lose an important clue as to whether the author has actually thought these things through. Investment blogs are already full of obvious AI output; judging whether an opinion is reliable can't rest on whether the prose is pretty, but on whether the view has a thinking process behind it.

item.title: China's Economic Peak Is Behind It: Credit Stalls, Deflation Ahead
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-geopoliticsdec-中国经济巅峰已过-美国优势还将扩大/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-geopoliticsdec-中国经济巅峰已过-美国优势还将扩大/
item.description: China's share of global GDP peaked in 2021 and has fallen since; credit growth has dropped from 18% to 5%, real growth may be just 1.5%-2%, and the US has outperformed for five straight years. The supply-chain-dominance narrative is falsified by the data; the future looks more like Japanese-style deflation.
item.content:encoded:
China's share of global GDP peaked in 2021 and has fallen since; credit growth has dropped from 18% to 5%, real growth may be just 1.5%-2%, and the US has outperformed for five straight years. The supply-chain-dominance narrative is falsified by the data; the future looks more like Japanese-style deflation.

It rebuts the mainstream narrative that China's new industries are a growth engine, grounding the call in credit, special bonds and demographic data — for anyone who wants to update their long-run view of the US and China.

0:05 China has already missed its window to overtake the US
Dmitri sets the frame with official data: China's share of global GDP peaked at 18.5% in 2021 and has declined every year since, while the US rose from 24% to about 26%. From this he concludes that not only is it nearly impossible for China to replace the US as the world's largest economy, but America's economic advantage may keep widening over the next decade. Logan agrees completely and steers the discussion toward a framework of ‘decay, not collapse.’

2:11 The root of China's slowdown is that credit expansion is over
Logan attributes China's slowdown to the end of extraordinary credit expansion. After the financial crisis China added credit equal to one-third of global GDP in eight years; credit growth averaged 18% from 2007-2016, fell to 9% after 2017, and is now slightly above 5%. Once credit stops, borrowers can no longer refinance and investment decelerates. Officials still report 5.2% growth for 2023 and 5% for 2024 and 2025, but he estimates real growth since 2022 at only 1.5%-2%, already below the US.

6:14 Scoring by purchasing power parity is rewarding deflation
To the common rebuttal that China has already overtaken the US on purchasing power parity, Logan says PPP comparisons still make sense for developing countries but do not hold between the world's two largest economies: scoring by PPP amounts to rewarding China for manufacturing deflation — the lower domestic prices are, the stronger the economy looks, and deflation is precisely the problem. He also stresses that debt is repaid in nominal local currency, so nominal GDP is what matters; and the exchange rate is not an exogenous variable but an external signal of China's policy capacity.

13:25 Capital controls are not a cure, they only buy time
Logan concedes that China's capital controls do work, but argues they are no panacea for a giant macro imbalance. The impossible trinity dictates that free capital flows, a stable exchange rate and independent monetary policy can be achieved at most two at a time. The function of capital controls is to slow outflows, suppress rapid cross-border volatility and channel outflows into channels the government can see — that Huawei and BYD can expand abroad on a large scale while the overseas M&A of private firms like HNA in 2016 was halted are two sides of this screening mechanism.

17:35 Credit is still subsidising old industries, not shifting to new ones
Logan rebuts the claim that credit is shifting toward higher-productivity new industries: central bank data show the share of loans issued at or below the Loan Prime Rate has risen from the low 20s% to 59%, meaning banks are continuously subsidising. The share of special revenue bonds going to so-called strategic industries rose only from about 2% to 6% between 2021 and 2025, with the vast majority still flowing to traditional sectors. Using the 2023 input-output tables, EVs, batteries, AI and solar together are about 6.3% of GDP, while the decline in property and infrastructure investment is roughly six times the increment from these new industries.

27:45 Europe is the last buyer of China's excess capacity
Logan judges that if Europe turns protectionist, China is ‘really finished’: the US market has already narrowed with limited room for transshipment, and the developing world cannot absorb China's excess capacity while sustaining its own growth. He warns that America's focus on the bilateral deficit is wrong — the deficit is determined by the savings-investment gap, and tariffs only redistribute it; failing to address the underlying imbalance will merely spawn more transshipment trade.

34:58 Without tax reform, domestic demand cannot get up
Logan compares the present to the Kosygin reform in the Soviet Union: Brezhnev chose the scientific-technological revolution over pushing reform and preserving ideology. For China to convert savings into consumption, the real lever is tax policy — extracting resources from high-net-worth individuals, state-owned enterprises and private firms shut out of the financial system. But he thinks it nearly unimaginable that Xi Jinping would go on television and declare that ‘the fiscal and financial system of the past 15 years no longer applies’; Beijing sticks to the 5% growth narrative partly to undermine export controls and deter Western investment in alternative supply chains.

39:00 China in 2035 will look like Japan today
Logan predicts that absent a dramatic policy shift, China's economy in 2035 will look more like Japan's: persistent deflation, persistent external surpluses, downward pressure on the exchange rate and low interest rates. The hardest constraint is demography — China's actual average age at death is 73, and the baby boom at the founding of the PRC will bring a population decline of 50-60 million over the next decade, about 3%-4% of the total; even holding the birth rate at last year's low of 7.92 million will not stop it. He also notes the fiscal deficit is already close to $2 trillion a year, 9.5% of GDP, leaving far fewer resources to draw on than in the past. Finally he says that if China really did win on export share, it would only provoke a stronger political backlash — ‘winning is losing.’

item.title: Bell Used Einstein's Own Tools to Refute His Core Argument
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-theoriesofever-贝尔用爱因斯坦自己的工具推翻了他的核心论点/

item.description: The EPR argument forces you to choose between "the quantum description is incomplete" and "action at a distance"; determinism was never a premise but an inferred conclusion. The full logic of Bell's theorem has to start here.
item.content:encoded:
The EPR argument forces you to choose between "the quantum description is incomplete" and "action at a distance"; determinism was never a premise but an inferred conclusion. The full logic of Bell's theorem has to start here.

Maudlin goes from the 1905 photoelectric effect all the way to the 1964 Bell inequality, breaking the EPR argument into steps you can check one by one. For anyone who wants to actually understand nonlocality rather than memorise conclusions.

3:05 The father of quantum theory is not Planck, it is Einstein
Although Planck is usually regarded as the father of quantum theory, the one who actually proposed the quantisation hypothesis was Einstein in his 1905 photoelectric effect paper. Planck only did statistical calculations, whereas Einstein explicitly argued that energy is transferred in discrete quanta. Maudlin deliberately corrects this historical attribution.

45:32 A single particle is enough to force action at a distance
Einstein's objection at the 1927 Solvay Conference was this: if the wave function completely describes a single particle, and the wave propagates in all directions toward the screen, then the particle might act at multiple locations simultaneously. To avoid multi-point action, one must introduce an instantaneous and global wave function collapse mechanism — which is precisely action at a distance. Note, this is not a question about faster-than-light signals.

1:14:50 If the wave function is real, locality has nowhere to live
The wave function of a multi-particle system is defined on configuration space rather than physical space; a two-particle system, for example, is a six-dimensional configuration space. In classical mechanics configuration space is merely a mathematical convenience, but if the wave function is regarded as fundamental reality, configuration space becomes the physical stage, and defining the locality of forces in each small region of that space becomes problematic. This is another layer of Einstein's worry about dynamical locality.

1:31:59 EPR's reality criterion cannot be coherently denied
EPR's reality criterion says: if one can predict with probability 1 the value of some physical quantity without disturbing the system, then that quantity corresponds to an element of physical reality. Maudlin stresses that this is a sufficient condition, not a necessary one. He rebuts the common attempts to deny the criterion, holding that it is analytic and cannot be coherently denied. This sets up the either/or conclusion that follows.

2:02:26 Either the description is incomplete, or accept action at a distance
Because the reality criterion cannot be denied, the EPR argument forces the situation into a binary choice: either accept that the quantum description is incomplete, or accept that Alice's operation in her lab really disturbs the physical state of Bob's particle, i.e. action at a distance. Einstein considered action at a distance absurd, so he chose incompleteness. This is the logical exit of the entire EPR argument.

2:10:34 Denying determinism cannot escape Bell's conclusion
Maudlin repeatedly stresses that in the EPR argument determinism is not assumed but inferred from perfect correlations and locality. He quotes Bell's own words: "Insofar as determinism plays a role in the EPR argument, it is not assumed but inferred." Therefore, trying to evade Bell's conclusion by denying determinism is completely ineffective.

2:43:53 Bohr's famous reply was in fact understood by no one
Faced with the EPR argument, Bohr had only two logically possible responses: accept action at a distance, or admit the quantum description is incomplete. But Bohr chose neither. Maudlin says his reply paper is "a mess" that no one can understand. He even mentions that in the volume edited by Wheeler and Zurek, two pages of Bohr's article are out of order, yet no one noticed, because no one could follow its logic at all.

2:55:02 No local theory can give the correct predictions
Bell's starting point was precisely the EPR paper, yet his conclusion was that Einstein's basic claim that "there is no action at a distance" is wrong: no local theory can produce the correct predictions. Maudlin calls this a huge ironic reversal — Bell used Einstein's own tools to refute his basic argument. This is the real entry point for understanding why Bell's theorem matters.

item.title: The quantum endgame isn't whose qubits are cleaner — it's who can mass-produce them on a phone-chip line
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-fromfirstprinc-硅自旋将赢-百万比特只需一块硅晶圆/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-fromfirstprinc-硅自旋将赢-百万比特只需一块硅晶圆/
item.description: The endgame of quantum computing isn't whose qubits are cleaner, it's who can mass-produce them on existing semiconductor lines; silicon spin qubits reuse TSMC's lithography, while trapped ions are stuck at a hundred thousand laser beams and superconductors at warehouse-scale refrigerators.
item.content:encoded:
The endgame of quantum computing isn't whose qubits are cleaner, it's who can mass-produce them on existing semiconductor lines; silicon spin qubits reuse TSMC's lithography, while trapped ions are stuck at a hundred thousand laser beams and superconductors at warehouse-scale refrigerators.

The exclusive value is in the back half: the CNOT error rate from the HRL paper, AI auto-tuning, FFP's astonishing scores; the first half's explanation of the principles leans popular-science, and veterans can fast-forward.

0:00 Trapped ions and superconductors must invent a miracle first; silicon doesn't
To build a hundred-thousand-qubit trapped-ion machine, you first have to invent the optical miracle of a hundred thousand laser beams; for a million superconducting qubits, you have to build a warehouse-sized cryostat; for a million spin qubits, you only need a standard 300mm silicon wafer, run through the same lithography equipment TSMC, ASML and Intel use to make phone processors. Krishna uses this to set the tone for the whole episode: the key to the quantum race isn't single-qubit fidelity, it's whether the path to scale already exists inside the industrial system.

32:48 Quantum computing has stopped comparing principles and started comparing engineering
In 2000 DiVincenzo proposed five criteria, with the aim of ruling out liquid-state NMR quantum computing. In this episode FFP proposes three criteria of its own: qubit quality, control, and scalability and economics. The rest of the episode is a point-by-point scoring of four routes: superconducting, trapped ion, neutral atom, and silicon spin. Laying out the evaluation framework itself tells you something: quantum computing has entered the stage of engineering competition, and you can't just talk about principles.

1:24:33 Superconducting isn't technically incapable, it just doesn't fit engineering-wise
Estimates suggest a thousand logical qubits would require ten million transmon physical qubits. The number of control lines is limited by the cooling capacity of the dilution refrigerator, frequencies are crowded, and helium-3 supply becomes a new resource constraint. FFP gives superconducting just 1/10 on scalability and economics, for a total of 11/30. This is the first time in the episode that "technically strong" and "engineering-wise infeasible" are scored separately; a warehouse-scale refrigerator means even a data center may not have room for it.

1:47:08 Trapped ions win on coherence time and lose on gate speed
Trapped-ion coherence times reach ten hours, but gate operations rely on phonons and are limited by the Paul trap's oscillation frequency, making them about a thousand times slower than superconducting. The result is counterintuitive: even if trapped ions could scale to encryption-breaking size, breaking 2048-bit RSA would take about a year, whereas superconducting would take only about eight hours. Long coherence time doesn't equal how much you can do per unit time; for practical computation, slow gate times are a throughput disaster overall.

2:03:32 The quantum threat is neither tomorrow nor forever
A March 2026 paper from Harvard, Caltech and Qera says ten thousand qubits might break internet encryption, but in practice it would take years; even with a hundred thousand physical qubits, breaking RSA under the mathematically optimal assumptions would take about three months. This number strikes at both extreme narratives at once: the quantum threat isn't tomorrow, but it is by no means forever distant. To achieve "breakable within months," qubit count, gate speed and error correction all have to hit the mark at the same time.

2:50:02 The life or death of quantum companies rests in government contracts
HRL lost key project funding in early 2026 and laid off 376 people. Government funding shifted from basic research toward applied research demanding rapid commercialisation; IBM and Intel received support under the CHIPS Act, and eventually IBM acquired HRL. Krishna calls this the debut of the quantum computing MVP: a quantum company's survival depends on government contracts, and being acquired isn't failure — it's letting the technology enter an industrial system with manufacturing capability.

3:23:10 A million qubits can't be tuned by hand; it has to go to image recognition
Automated tuning becomes the key to scaling: a 2023 paper had only six electron spins that could be tuned by hand, and hand-tuning a million qubits would take a human lifetime. Tuning is essentially image recognition — when you sweep the voltage, tunnelling events show up as stripes, and Krishna's team uses DETR, combining ResNet and a Transformer, to automatically recognise the stripes and generate parameters. This is also the hidden premise of why silicon spin can reuse semiconductor lines: no matter how many qubits there are, software can align them automatically.

3:32:31 Silicon may not be first to be made, but it will be the last to win
FFP's final scores: silicon spin gets 10/10 on qubit quality, 10/10 on control (provided the isotope enrichment and valley state problems are solved), 10000/10 on scalability and economics, for a total of 10020/30; by contrast neutral atoms score minus 3000. Krishna admits silicon may not be the first route to achieve fault tolerance, but once it does, being cheap and easy to manufacture will make it the final standard, just as the transistor replaced the vacuum tube.

item.title: AI chip shipments are about to jump an order of magnitude: from a million units to 15 million
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-techtechpotato-未来-ai-定制芯片的形态-一只带-16-个-hbm-的巨兽/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-techtechpotato-未来-ai-定制芯片的形态-一只带-16-个-hbm-的巨兽/
item.description: Broadcom's president lays out the AI chip roadmap: from a million units to 15 million, with "beast" as the largest package at 8 stackable compute dies plus 16 HBM, and four of the five frontier labs working with the company.
item.content:encoded:
Broadcom's president lays out the AI chip roadmap: from a million units to 15 million, with "beast" as the largest package at 8 stackable compute dies plus 16 HBM, and four of the five frontier labs working with the company.

Broadcom rarely discloses anything, yet here it gives three package tiers and three shipment tiers, plus a clear call on the HBM bottleneck; for anyone tracking ASICs and packaging, these 11 minutes carry more information than a lot of long-form analysis.

1:06 Companies designing their own chips still outsource the last step
Google, Meta, Amazon and some frontier model companies can all have their own chip design teams, set their own architecture and interconnect, but in the end they still have to "get the thing built": deal with the foundry and the development kit, and manage the timing and latency of the connections between transistors. Broadcom is the largest of the back-end design service providers that charge for this kind of work. Customers go to it not just for design capability but for a batch of ready-made IP such as high-speed I/O, high-speed compute and memory controllers.

3:09 The least talkative chip company suddenly started talking about itself
Broadcom is a mystery to the outside world: it has almost no PR department and rarely discloses anything on its own initiative. Occasionally it ships a Tomahawk networking chip, or chats with Patrick Kennedy on ServeTheHome. Over the past year, president Charlie has unusually taken the stage at launch events to talk about what Broadcom is doing and why it is expanding its customer base from traditional networking chips to custom AI chips. This slide showing three tiers of chips is the clue.

4:09 Today's AI servers are only the smallest of the three tiers
Of the three tiers Charlie showed, the leftmost one is already shipping in hundreds of thousands of systems, about the size of the Cisco chip on the table: one compute die in the middle, four to six HBM around it, using a TSMC CoWoS-like package. Broadcom says that over the past year it has shipped more than a million of these chips for customers. This tier is the reality of today's AI servers.

5:09 The bigger the package, the higher the shipment volume
The middle tier is noticeably larger: two to four compute/IO dies with eight to twelve HBM around them, a form factor that also covers AMD's MI455X. The shipment expectations Charlie gave are the key: 5 million units for the middle tier, and 15 million units for the rightmost tier. Set next to "a million units over the past year", this is not linear growth — it is next-generation custom AI chip shipments jumping a full order of magnitude.

6:11 The rightmost one may be compute die stacked on compute die
The rightmost beast: the red is eight compute dies, arranged in two columns of four, and they are stacked. Charlie lifts the red to reveal purple underneath, which could be SRAM, or SRAM could be on top; if it is compute-on-compute, that is effectively sixteen compute dies. Each compute die gets two HBM, so one package holds sixteen HBM modules, with two light-blue IO dies at the top and bottom ends, and openings left at the package edge for optical modules.

7:11 Nearly every frontier model company is building its own chip
Charlie said that four of the five leading frontier model labs are working with Broadcom on custom compute chips. Companies like OpenAI and Anthropic define the design they want, Broadcom does the back-end work and interfaces with TSMC, and then partners like Supermicro and WiWynn put it into data centers and deploy it at scale. This also explains why Broadcom is expanding capacity: it not only serves traditional networking customers but is also taking orders from large model companies.

9:11 What blocks the ramp may not be packaging but HBM
The real bottleneck may not be packaging but whether there is enough high-bandwidth memory to go around: will a new form factor emerge outside HBM, sitting between DDR/LPDDR and HBM, to fill the gap? Separately, Broadcom said on stage that it has already deployed a 2nm chip with a partner, slightly smaller than beast and closer in time. That is a reminder that over the next few years, advanced packaging and HBM capacity will get swept up along with custom chip orders.

10:13 The first 2nm custom chip to land may come from Japan
The host pinned down the "coming soon, slightly smaller" 2nm chip Broadcom mentioned: he asked George of Chips and Cheese, and the two concluded it is Fujitsu's Monaka — a 2nm compute die paired with a 5nm SRAM die, with a central IO die in between. The chip has already appeared at several conferences as a mockup or test silicon.

Percy Fawcett's Amazon expeditions are usually told as adventure legend, but the real starting point was a border dispute driven by the rubber trade; his "respect" for Indigenous peoples is badly oversimplified, and the City of Z that consumed him may rest on a forged manuscript.

This episode has medium information density, but it lays out the rubber trade, the Indigenous catastrophe and the opening of Manuscript 512 clearly; readers who only want adventure anecdotes may find the first half slow going.

3:04 His obsession began with a Roman well in his childhood
Fawcett was born in 1867. His family was aristocratic in name, but his father Edward Fawcett had already squandered the fortune and could only serve as private assistant to Queen Victoria's son "Bertie" (the future Edward VII). Fawcett described his childhood in Torquay as lacking parental affection, which made him introverted. His sister recalled that as a boy he found a well full of Roman pottery on Halden Moors and had his siblings lower him down to retrieve the treasures and send them to a museum. That boldness, stubbornness and hunger for the world outside would reappear later in his devotion to the occult and to the Amazon.

8:13 The officer who held séances still made major
In 1901 Fawcett married Nina; in 1903 his eldest son Jack was born, and that same year he was posted to Spike Island off the south coast of Ireland. Fawcett found the posting dull, so he spent his free time holding séances. His interest in the occult was not a side note; his son Brian later wrote that anyone seeking knowledge beyond the material world might be called a mystic. Nor did it block his military advancement — he was promoted to major. Fawcett's "rationality" and "superstition" coexisted, setting up his later unshakeable faith in Manuscript 512.

10:19 His first trip to the Amazon was diplomacy, not adventure
In 1901 Fawcett joined the Royal Geographical Society and completed specialist training in boundary demarcation. In 1906 the society's president, Sir George Goldie, summoned him, asked what he knew about Bolivia, and then told him: the border dispute among Brazil, Peru and Bolivia had escalated because of the rubber trade, and the countries involved would not accept a demarcation by any party with a stake in it, so the Bolivian government had asked the Royal Geographical Society to arbitrate and recommend an officer. For Fawcett this was a chance to "escape the monotony of an artillery officer's life"; he was 39, and his wife was pregnant with their second child. The chain of argument here is: the economic value of rubber → territorial dispute → Britain intervening as a "disinterested" third party → Fawcett entering the Amazon as a surveyor. The counterintuitive point is that his first expedition was not a self-directed adventure but a commercial and diplomatic arrangement.

14:25 He was attacked everywhere because nine in ten locals were already dead
Before he reached South America, the rubber industry had already transformed the region. The figures cited in the episode show that before Europeans arrived, the area of present-day Brazil held at least 2,000 Indigenous tribes with a total population of roughly 11 million; in the first hundred years after the colonists arrived in the 16th century, 90% of Indigenous people died of disease or genocide, and survivors were often enslaved to work rubber. The rubber trade made land extremely valuable, Europeans moved in and seized Indigenous land, and Indigenous people came to see all Europeans as a threat — that is the background to the hostility Fawcett encountered. His own accounts also prove he knew clearly about the atrocities of European colonists. This is the structural explanation of "why he was attacked everywhere," and it corrects the romanticised narrative of the explorer in peril.

17:28 Saying he respected Indigenous people sets the bar far too low
Fawcett did not only confront Indigenous people. He would require himself and his companions to lay down their weapons and show they posed no threat, he learned local languages, and he condemned the earlier European colonists for creating and worsening the problem. At the same time, the mass of his writing was "extremely racist" and condescending. The host states plainly that later generations often say he "respected Indigenous peoples," and that this is an oversimplification; even if he was "better much of the time" than European explorers of his era, that baseline is terrifyingly low. The value of this point: much popular narrative today casts Fawcett as an enlightened explorer, and the episode dismantles that myth with concrete textual evidence, without reducing his behaviour to that of an outright villain.

19:28 He broke an ambush with an accordion, not a gun
This is one of Fawcett's most famous escapes. His expedition was ambushed on a river by Indigenous archers, and calls for peace had no effect. He had his companion Todd sit on a log mid-sandbar with an accordion and start playing, while the others sang loudly and stamped their feet. Before long the arrows stopped, a wide-eyed Indigenous man peered out from the bushes, and the expedition was welcomed into the village and given help. The example shows Fawcett did not only resort to force — his tool for solving the problem was music and clowning; it also shows his records contain both observations worth taking seriously and a great deal of unreliable exaggeration, setting up the later comparisons with the giant snake, the peanuts and the two-nosed dog.

25:32 He believed in a lost city because old documents really described one
Before the First World War, Fawcett was completing his mapping efficiently (usually far faster than expected) while growing ever more obsessed with the idea of a lost city in the jungle. He named the city he was looking for Zed, fixing its location in Mato Grosso, the non-coastal state in southern Brazil; the state covers about 900,000 square kilometres, is densely forested, and remains the least densely populated region of Brazil today, with almost no Europeans entering it in the early 20th century. The chain of argument here is: a large body of 16th- and 17th-century Spanish and Portuguese explorers' documents recorded "very advanced large cities" → Fawcett believed they really existed → he became ever more fixated on finding the City of Z.

29:40 The manuscript he believed without reservation may be a hoax
After the war Fawcett kept studying old documents, and the one most often mentioned is Manuscript 512, held at the National Library in Rio de Janeiro: a Portuguese adventurer's 1753 account of what he saw in the Amazon, whose author is sometimes said to be João de Silvestre de Moraes. Fawcett gave the author the pseudonym Francisco Raposo and wrote in his article that he believed the manuscript's contents "without reservation," calling it an "incomparable story." But the host had already warned at the start of the episode that the document "is very likely a hoax." So the whole suspense is not "does the lost city exist" but why a geographically trained officer would become so obsessed with a possibly forged 1753 record.
