item.content:encoded:
Jim Al-Khalili argues that time is real and directed, that irreversibility is more fundamental than time-symmetric equations, and proposes replacing thermodynamic entropy with quantum entanglement entropy as the basis for the past hypothesis.

Sean Carroll and Jim Al-Khalili hold opposite positions on the arrow of time, and this episode exposes where they genuinely diverge; the second half also covers quantum biology mechanisms and a new hypothesis about quantum entanglement entropy.

4:07 Time's direction is built in, not emergent
Jim stakes out a hard position: time is real and tangible, part of four-dimensional spacetime, not merely something a clock measures. He goes further, saying time's directionality is not emergent from directionless fundamental laws but is built into the universe. Sean reminds the audience this is in fact a major controversy — many physicists hold that time is just a tool or that its direction is a product of coarse-graining. Jim's intuition is that if we look from inside the universe, irreversibility is the more fundamental thing.

17:38 No system is isolated, so irreversibility is the norm
The traditional narrative: fundamental equations like Newton's and Schrödinger's are invariant under time reversal, so the arrow of time must emerge from entropy increase or coarse-graining. Jim inverts this, arguing that time-symmetric equations are only an idealization, because no system is truly isolated — even quantum systems are constantly entangling with their environment. Time-symmetric equations apply only to isolated systems and are a special case of the master equation; in reality everything exchanges energy and information with its environment, and irreversibility is the norm. He concedes this is a minority position, but thinks it is the foundation closer to the real world.

27:50 The special moment can only go at the Big Bang, not last week
If the entire universe is treated as an isolated system that also obeys time-symmetric laws, then by the second law, yesterday's entropy should be higher than today's, not lower. The only way out is to push that special moment back to the very beginning: the Big Bang. This is the past hypothesis. Jim stresses it is not an extra assumption but part of the universe's initial conditions, on a par with fine-tuning of constants. He agrees with Sean: if you must pick a special moment, the Big Bang is far more reasonable than last week.

31:03 The laws contain no flow of time, yet we feel one
Even if low-entropy initial conditions explain the arrow of time, Sean presses: where do psychological experiences like ‘now’ and the sense of passage come from? Jim honestly admits that the laws of physics contain no flow of time, yet we feel time flowing. He calls this the gap between physical time and manifest time, and says he is not even sure how to state it clearly. That candour is more valuable than pretending to have solved it, and it shows the problem of time is far from closed.

45:51 A DNA mutation may come from one proton's quantum tunnelling
Jim, from the perspective of a nuclear physicist, gives quantum biology's most concrete case: the two strands of the DNA double helix are joined by hydrogen bonds, and a hydrogen atom is essentially a proton. Löwdin proposed in the early 1960s that a proton might tunnel through the energy barrier to the opposite strand, causing a mutation during replication. Jim's team has run increasingly refined calculations to pin down the ratio of tunnelling to thermal excitation. He points out that quantum biology is not the old line that ‘atoms are themselves quantum’, but asks whether life has evolved tricks that exploit long-lived coherence and entanglement.

1:03:12 A more fundamental version of the past hypothesis is entanglement entropy
The thermodynamic past hypothesis requires specifying a low-entropy microstate. Jim and philosopher Eddy Chen tried a more quantum version: assume the universe began in a pure state with extremely low entanglement entropy, with subsystems barely entangled with one another. As it evolves, subsystems gradually entangle, and the universe's total entanglement entropy rises monotonically. Conceptually this is more fundamental than thermodynamic entropy, but Jim admits there are still many holes — such as how finely subsystems should be divided. This direction is not finished.

1:12:29 After cosmic heat death, time still passes
Many say time may disappear at extreme scales. Jim counters: even if the universe reaches thermal equilibrium in tens of trillions of years, with no change available to measure time by, time still passes. He concedes this is not time that holds in every reference frame in the relativistic sense, but it brings time almost back to Newton's absolute clock — a genuinely occurring event. For him, even if time emerges from something more fundamental, that does not make it unreal.
